items.title: Rapid and robust effects of high-dose intermittent Transcranial Brain Stimulation (iTBS) on depression and suicidal ideation in adolescents with acute major depression: a 10-day randomised, controlled, single-blind trial.
items.authors: Yang Y, Ye Q, Peng Z, Cai W, Wen J, Zhang J, Lan Y.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Depression is extremely common among adolescents and can significantly increase the risk of suicide when severe. High-dose intermittent theta burst stimulation (iTBS) is a secure and efficacious physical treatment. However, clinical evidence in adolescents remains limited. This research is designed to assess the therapeutic impacts of high-dose iTBS on depressive symptoms, anxiety symptoms, and suicidal ideation in adolescents suffering from acute depression, along with the factors linked to treatment response.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: A total of 61 patients were randomly assigned to either the high-dose iTBS group or the sham stimulation group. All participants received 10 daily sessions of high dose iTBS stimulation over a two-week period, targeting the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC). Outcome measures assessed at baseline, post-intervention, and 1-month follow-up included 24-item Hamilton Depression Rating Scale (HAMD-24) scores, Beck Scale for Suicide Ideation - Chinese Version (BSI-CV), and Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale (HAMA). Clinical factors influencing iTBS efficacy were further analyzed.

sections.heading: Result
sections.text: At the end of the 10-day intervention, the high-dose iTBS group exhibited significantly lower HAMD-24 (p = 0.008, Cohen`s d = 0.71 [95%CI: 0.188-1.224]) and BSI-CV (p = 0.011, Cohen`s d = 0.67[95%CI: 0.154-1.186]) scores compared with the sham group, and this advantage persisted at the 1-month follow-up (Week 6) (HAMD-24: Cohen`s d = 0.96[ 95%CI: 0.43-1.49]; BSI-CV: Cohen`s d = 0.76[95%CI: 0.24-1.28]). In contrast, between-group differences in HAMA scores were non-significant both post-intervention (Week 2) and at the 1-month follow-up (Week 6) (p > 0.05). Moreover, poorer family functioning within the high-dose iTBS cohort was associated with diminished therapeutic benefit (p < 0.05).

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: Current research indicates that a 10-day course of high-dose iTBS is effective in alleviating depressive symptoms and suicidal ideation in adolescents with depression, and that the therapeutic effects persist for up to one month after the end of treatment. We also found that high-dose iTBS was less effective in patients with poor baseline family functioning.

sections.text: Chinese clinical trial Registry (ChiCTR2500101152), trial registration date: April 21, 2025(retrospectively registered).

items.title: Clinical outcomes of subtalar arthrodesis for calcaneal fracture malunion and their association with preoperative anxiety and depression: a retrospective cohort study.
items.authors: Zhao H, Lu J, Li Y, Hu D, Xu J.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Patients with foot and ankle disorders often experience preoperative anxiety / depression, which can adversely affect surgical outcomes. This study aimed to explore the factors influencing preoperative mental health status in patients with malunited calcaneal fractures and to evaluate the potential impact of preoperative mental health on prognosis following subtalar arthrodesis (STA).

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: This study retrospectively enrolled 45 patients with malunited calcaneal fractures who underwent subtalar arthrodesis from January 2015 to May 2023. Demographic data were collected, and assessments using the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS), American Orthopaedic Foot & Ankle Society (AOFAS) ankle-hindfoot score, and Visual Analog Scale (VAS) were performed. The Wilcoxon signed-rank test was used to compare preoperative and final follow-up VAS and AOFAS scores. Spearman correlation was used to analyze the associations between preoperative HADS scores and preoperative VAS/AOFAS scores, and the associations between preoperative HADS scores and final follow-up VAS/AOFAS scores. A HADS-A or HADS-D score ≥ 8 was defined as indicating anxiety/depressive symptoms.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: A total of 39 patients (32 male, 7 female) completed follow-up. Sixteen patients (41.03%) had preoperative HADS-A or HADS-D scores ≥ 8, indicating anxiety/depressive symptoms. Significant improvements in VAS and AOFAS scores were observed at final follow-up compared to preoperative assessments (P < 0.001). Preoperative VAS scores showed significant positive correlations with both anxiety and depressive symptoms (P < 0.05), while preoperative AOFAS scores showed a significant negative correlation with anxiety (P < 0.05) but not with depression (P > 0.05). No significant correlations were found between preoperative anxiety/depressive symptoms and baseline characteristics (gender, age, BMI, disease duration; all P > 0.05). Notably, preoperative HADS scores were not significantly correlated with final follow-up VAS or AOFAS scores (all P > 0.05).

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: STA effectively treats malunited calcaneal fractures, significantly improving clinical outcomes. Preoperative pain levels correlated with both anxiety and depressive symptoms, whereas functional status correlated only with anxiety. No statistically significant association was identified between preoperative anxiety/depressive symptoms and final follow-up pain relief or functional recovery in this cohort. Given the modest sample size, these null findings should be interpreted cautiously. Clinicians should prioritize preoperative pain management to alleviate psychological distress and optimize perioperative care.

items.title: Childhood Trauma Exposure Associated With a More Severe Course of Metabolic Disturbances in Bipolar Disorder: A 36-Month Longitudinal Prospective Cohort Study.
items.authors: Galvez-Florez JF, Guillen-Burgos HF, Moreno-López S, Ramírez-Posada M, Anaya JM, McIntyre RS.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Childhood trauma (CT) is a recognized risk factor for adverse psychiatric and physical health outcomes in individuals with bipolar disorder (BD). However, few prospective studies have examined how CT relates to the longitudinal course of metabolic dysregulation in BD. This study aimed to describe the association between CT exposure and the progression of metabolic disturbances over 36 months in adults with BD.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: In this prospective cohort study, 305 adults diagnosed with BD (Types I and II) were followed across 13 visits over 36 months. Participants were stratified according to CT exposure using the Childhood Trauma Questionnaire-Short Form (CTQ-SF). Metabolic outcomes (HbA1c, BMI, total cholesterol, HDL cholesterol, LDL cholesterol, triglycerides, and hs-CRP) were analyzed with inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) and linear mixed-effects models incorporating a group-by-time interaction.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Of the 305 participants enrolled, 53 (17.4%) were lost to follow-up. Longitudinal analyses showed significant CT-by-time interactions for all metabolic markers (p < 0.001). At 36 months, participants exposed to CT showed greater increases than non-exposed participants in HbA1c (adjusted least-squares mean difference 1.11%, 95% CI 0.89-1.33), BMI (4.46 kg/m^2, 95% CI 3.90-5.03), and hs-CRP (2.68 mg/L, 95% CI 2.52-2.84), together with unfavorable changes in the lipid profile. Effect sizes were large (Cohen's d > 0.8). These associations persisted after IPTW weighting for measured baseline covariates.

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: In this observational cohort, CT exposure was associated with an accelerated trajectory of metabolic deterioration in individuals with BD after weighting for measured baseline characteristics. Because the design is observational and several behavioral, socioeconomic, and illness-course determinants of metabolic risk were not measured, these findings should be interpreted as associations rather than as causal effects. They nonetheless support the value of early trauma-informed assessment and of integrated care strategies addressing both psychiatric and physical health in BD. Future research should incorporate detailed lifestyle and treatment-exposure data, additional inflammatory biomarkers, and preventive interventions to mitigate long-term cardiometabolic risk in this vulnerable population.

items.title: HADS-Assessed Anxiety/Depression Status and Ocular Outcomes in Vision-Threatening Diabetic Retinopathy: A Multicenter Retrospective Cohort Study.
items.authors: Li B, Jiang Y, Li C, Huang Y, Zhao S, Zhou C, Zheng Z, Zhang X.

sections.heading: Purpose
sections.text: Vision-threatening diabetic retinopathy (VTDR) poses significant blindness risks and the study aimed to identify the impact of psychological factors on its ocular outcomes.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: This retrospective cohort study enrolled 782 VTDR patients from three ophthalmological centers (2018-2021). DR severity was graded using ETDRS criteria. Primary outcomes included tractional retinal detachment (TRD) involving the fovea, neovascular glaucoma (NVG), final best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) <0.3, and recurrent vitreous hemorrhage (VH). Anxiety and depression were assessed via the hospital anxiety and depression scale (HADS). Univariable and multivariable logistic regression evaluated the associations between HADS scores and ocular outcomes.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: After a median follow-up of 24.8 months, depressive symptoms (HADS-D ≥8) were associated with higher rates of BCVA <0.3 (67.8% vs. 57.2%, p = 0.033) and NVG (13.6% vs. 6.9%, p = 0.020). Recurrent VH was more frequent in patients with anxiety (21.0% vs. 10.6%, p = 0.031) or depression (20.3% vs. 10.7%, p = 0.045). Multivariable logistic analysis revealed that each 1-point increase in HADS-D score significantly increased adjusted odds of TRD (aOR = 1.06, 95% CI: 1.01-1.11), BCVA <0.3 (aOR = 1.07, 95% CI: 1.02-1.11), recurrent VH (aOR = 1.09, 95% CI: 1.02-1.17), and NVG (aOR = 1.10, 95% CI: 1.03-1.17; all p < 0.05). There was a consistent positive gradient between HADS severity and adverse outcomes.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: Depressive symptoms are independently associated with worse ocular prognoses in VTDR patients. Systematic psychological screening and intervention is essential to mitigate vision deterioration risk in this population.

items.title: Combining Cognitive Training and Brain Stimulation: A Novel Approach to Address Disordered Eating and Antipsychotic-Induced Weight Gain in People With Severe Mental Illness.
items.authors: Lopes M, Monssen D, Grycuk L, Gordon G, Gaughran F, Campbell IC, Schmidt U.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Antipsychotic-induced weight gain is a distressing side effect that most often occurs within the first 3-6 months of pharmacological initiation, significantly increasing cardiometabolic risk and mortality in individuals with severe mental illness.

sections.heading: Aims
sections.text: To assess the feasibility of reducing food craving and binge eating using Approach Bias Modification Training (ABMT) combined with real or sham Transcranial Direct Current Stimulation (tDCS).

sections.heading: Method
sections.text: In this double-blind, parallel-group, two-arm, sham-controlled trial, adults with schizophrenia/schizoaffective disorder on stable doses of antipsychotics were randomly allocated to a total of five ABMT sessions together with either real or sham tDCS administered over 3 weeks. Assessments were made at baseline (T0), post-treatment (T1) and at a 2-week follow-up (T2). Feasibility outcomes included recruitment, attendance, retention, tDCS safety, acceptability, tolerability, and blinding. Secondary outcomes were changes in food craving, binge eating, approach bias to food, body mass index, and psychological symptoms.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Twenty-eight participants were recruited (93% of target). Retention was high (T1 = 85.7% and T2 = 78.6%); blinding accuracy was 46.4%. Medium effect sizes favoured 'ABMT + real tDCS' for reducing binge eating (d = -0.6, 95% CI -1.5, 0.3), and 'ABMT + sham tDCS' for reducing food cravings (d = 0.5, 95% CI -0.4, 1.4). Within-groups, only the 'ABMT + real tDCS' arm showed reduced approach bias to food and approach-avoidance bias to food, and increased avoidance bias to food (all p < 0.05). This was followed by reduced binge eating episodes (p < 0.05). Both groups reported frequent binge-eating episodes ('ABMT + tDCS' = 43%; 'ABMT + sham tDCS' = 28.6%).

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: The initiation of antipsychotic therapy is a critical clinical window for early intervention to mitigate the long-term metabolic and psychiatric consequences of antipsychotic-induced weight gain. Combining ABMT + tDCS is acceptable and may help reduce binge eating in individuals on antipsychotics, with a potential synergistic effect between cognitive training and brain stimulation. A confirmatory trial is needed to assess its effectiveness and should include BED diagnosis as a stratification criterion.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Decentralized (ie, fully remote) clinical trials (DCTs) offer a scalable and ecologically valid approach to evaluating digital mental health interventions (DMHIs). Yet, incorporating objective measures of well-being within DCTs poses novel methodological and feasibility challenges that can limit the rigor and precision of data collection in the field.

sections.heading: Objective

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: The BeWell Study methodology is described. Descriptive statistics characterized recruitment and retention, as well as data completion and data quality. sections.heading: Results

items.title: Serum ferritin and hematological indices in children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder: a matched case-control study.
items.authors: Abbasi E, Abdi A, Farshi M.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: ADHD is a common neurodevelopmental disorder with substantial clinical heterogeneity. Iron is essential for brain development and dopaminergic function, and altered iron homeostasis may contribute to ADHD pathophysiology. However, evidence on peripheral iron biomarkers remains inconsistent. To compare iron-related biomarkers and hematological indices between children with ADHD and neurotypical controls and to assess whether serum ferritin is independently associated with ADHD.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: This age- and sex-frequency-matched case-control study included 50 children with ADHD recruited from the pediatric neurology and child psychiatry outpatient clinics and 50 neurotypical controls recruited from the general pediatric outpatient clinic of the same tertiary hospital between March 2023 and March 2024. Serum ferritin, serum iron, total iron-binding capacity (TIBC), hemoglobin, mean corpuscular volume (MCV), mean corpuscular hemoglobin (MCH), and mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration (MCHC) were measured using standardized laboratory methods. Group comparisons were performed using independent-samples t tests and chi-square tests. Multivariable logistic regression was used to examine the independent association between ferritin and ADHD after adjustment for relevant covariates.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Children with ADHD had significantly lower serum ferritin levels than controls (38.4 ± 17.4 vs. 51.2 ± 19.8 ng/mL; p < 0.001). Serum iron was also lower in the ADHD group (83.3 ± 25.0 vs. 97.6 ± 22.4 µg/dL; p = 0.004), whereas TIBC was higher (356 ± 48 vs. 334 ± 42 µg/dL; p = 0.019). Iron deficiency (ferritin < 30 ng/mL) was more common in children with ADHD (34.0% vs. 14.0%; p = 0.018). Hemoglobin, MCV, MCH, and MCHC did not differ significantly between groups. In multivariable analysis, lower ferritin remained independently associated with ADHD (adjusted OR = 1.42 per 10 ng/mL decrease; 95% CI: 1.08-1.86; p = 0.011).

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: Children with ADHD had lower iron stores despite largely normal routine hematological indices. These findings support a potential role for altered iron metabolism in ADHD and suggest that ferritin assessment may provide clinically useful information beyond routine blood counts.

items.title: Neuropsychiatric adverse event reporting with GLP-1-based therapies: a post-marketing pharmacovigilance analysis using the WHO global individual case safety report database (VigiBase).
items.authors: Liang J, Bo L, Miao X, Guo X, Xu J, He J, Ye X.

sections.heading: Objective
sections.text: Concerns regarding neuropsychiatric adverse events (NPAEs), including depression and suicidality, have emerged with the expanding use of GLP-1-based therapies across metabolic and weight-management indications. This study aimed to characterize neuropsychiatric adverse-event reporting patterns for GLP-1-based therapies in VigiBase using disproportionality analysis.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: Individual case safety reports entered into the WHO global pharmacovigilance database (VigiBase) from inception through 31 January 2025 were examined. Disproportionality analysis using the information components and the reporting odds ratio was conducted to identify putative safety signals. The full VigiBase reporting background during the study period was used as the comparator. We described the drug-event pairs, mapped signal overlap across agents, evaluated the relationship between reporting frequency and signal magnitude, and conducted stratified analyses by sex and age.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Among 899 280 GLP-1RAs-related reports, 19 811 (2.2%) related NPAEs comprised 273 preferred terms and generated 69 positive signals. Semaglutide and liraglutide presented the broadest and most potent signal portfolios, driven chiefly by binge eating (semaglutide, IC₀₂₅ = 3.379; ROR₀₂₅ = 14.483), and aversion (liraglutide, IC₀₂₅ = 3.365; ROR₀₂₅ = 20.512). In contrast, albiglutide was essentially signal negative, and dulaglutide and tirzepatide generated narrower spectra. In addition, semaglutide was positively associated with two "suicide/self-injury" AEs: "depression suicidal" (ROR₀₂₅ = 4.822) and "suicidal ideation" (ROR₀₂₅ = 2.643).

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: This study identified several potential drug safety signals. However, the estimates were unadjusted and may be influenced by confounding by indication, channelling, notoriety bias, and event competition. Eating-related signals should be interpreted cautiously because they may overlap with the treated population and appetite-related pharmacology of these agents. Given the spontaneous reporting nature of VigiBase, these findings should be interpreted as potential reporting signals rather than evidence of causality. Further well-designed observational studies and prospective clinical investigations are needed to clarify whether GLP-1-based therapies are associated with increased neuropsychiatric risk and to identify patient-level risk modifiers.

items.title: Association between stressful life events and psychoactive substance use in adolescents and young adults from Argentina, Colombia and Peru.
items.authors: Paredes-Angeles R, Lazo-Porras M, Carbonel A, Gómez-Restrepo C, Brusco LI, Sureshkumar DS, Uribe-Restrepo JM, Olivar N, Fung C, Esnal F, Godoy-Casasbuenas N, Priebe S, Diez-Canseco F.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Substance use is a common problem among young people in Latin America and has significant consequences for their mental health. One of the variables associated with the use of psychoactive substances is stressful life events (SLEs). SLEs can include traumatic experiences, significant losses, interpersonal conflicts, financial difficulties, among others.

sections.heading: Objective
sections.text: To explore the association between the number of SLEs and psychoactive substance use in adolescents and young adults from deprived urban settings.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: In this cross-sectional study, adolescents and young adults were recruited from disadvantaged urban environments in Buenos Aires, Bogota and Lima. Data were collected between April 2021 and November 2022. The number of SLEs experienced in lifetime until a year ago was assessed using an adaptation of the Adolescent Appropriate Life Events Scale, which asks about 30 SLEs. Psychoactive substance use in the last three months was self-rated and six outcomes were analyzed: alcohol, tobacco, marijuana, tranquilizers, other drugs, and use of three or more substances. Crude and adjusted prevalence ratios (PRs) were estimated using generalized linear models of the Poisson family with log link and robust variances for each outcome.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: 2378 participants' data were analyzed. Participants experiencing between 10 and 22 SLEs more than a year ago had higher prevalence rates of psychoactive substance use than participants between 0 and 5 SLEs in four of six outcomes: tobacco (PR: 1.69, 95% CI 1.37-2.08), alcohol (PR: 1.23, 95% CI 1.13-1.35), marijuana (PR: 1.75, 95% CI 1.35-2.26), and three or more psychoactive substances (PR: 1.85, 95% CI 1.35-2.53) in the last three months.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: Experiencing a higher number of SLEs was associated with the use of tobacco, alcohol, marijuana, and three or more psychoactive substances in adolescents and young adults from disadvantaged urban areas of Bogota, Buenos Aires, and Lima. Recognizing young people who have gone through multiple stressful life events at an early stage is essential, so that interventions can be implemented to prevent them from turning to psychoactive substances.

items.title: Factors associated with suicidal ideation among Malaysian university students: Dynamics of mental health vulnerabilities and protective resources.
items.authors: Wu SL, Mah PN, Tan SA, Fam JY, Yap CC.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Suicidal ideation is a major public health concern among university students, especially in recent years. Guided by Beck's cognitive model of suicidal behaviour and the dual-factor model of mental health, this study examined the association between mental health vulnerabilities (i.e., depression, anxiety, stress and pessimism), protective resources (i.e., social support and optimism) and suicidal ideation among Malaysian university students.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: Data were collected in 2023 using a cross-sectional survey design. A total of 547 university students aged 18 to 24 years old (M = 21.23, SD = 1.82) completed the Suicidal Ideation Attributes Scale (SIDAS), Depression Anxiety Stress Scale-21, Revised Life Orientation Test, and Multidimensional Scale of Perceived Social Support. Pearson correlation analysis was conducted to examine relationships among the study variables, while binary logistic regression was used to identify factors associated with the presence of suicidal ideation. The SIDAS score was dichotomised as 0= no suicidal ideation and > 0 as the presence of any suicidal ideation.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Nearly half of the participants reported some degree of suicidal ideation. Correlation analyses showed that depression, anxiety, stress, and pessimism were positively correlated with suicidal ideation, while optimism and social support were negatively correlated with suicidal ideation. In the logistic regression model, pessimism, depression, anxiety and social support remained significant factors associated with suicidal ideation.

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: The findings suggest that suicidal ideation among Malaysian university students is associated with both psychological vulnerabilities and interpersonal resources. Interventions should not focus solely on reducing psychological distress but should also address pessimistic thinking patterns and strengthen perceived social support. Given the cross-sectional design and convenience sampling approach, the findings should be interpreted as associations rather than causal relationships.

items.title: Network analysis of the relationship between anxiety, depression and resilience in patients with pancreatic cancer and gender differences.
items.authors: Cheng H, Zhuang X, Zhao Y, He Q, Zhang H, Han Y.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Pancreatic cancer patients demonstrate elevated vulnerability to depression and anxiety relative to other gastrointestinal malignancies, attributable to the disease's dismal prognosis and substantial symptom burden. However, symptom-level relationships among anxiety, depression, and resilience in pancreatic cancer remain insufficiently understood. Therefore, this study employed network analysis to investigate the interrelationships among anxiety, depression, and psychological resilience in the population. Additionally, a comparative analysis of the network structure was conducted to explore gender differences. Ultimately, this study aims to provide theory-driven intervention strategies and practical guidelines for supporting the mental health of patients diagnosed with pancreatic cancer.

sections.heading: Method
sections.text: This cross-sectional study enrolled 759 patients with pancreatic cancer from Guangzhou, China, between June 2024 and July 2025. Anxiety, depression, and resilience were assessed using the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS) and Brief Resilience Scale (BRS). A regularized partial correlation network was constructed based on the survey data, and the bridge expected influence index was applied to quantify the bridge components. We also compared the network structures of male and female samples to explore sex differences.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: The prevalence rates of anxiety and depression were 24.2% and 30.3%, respectively. A7 "Panic" (0.903) was the core symptom in the anxiety, depression, and resilience symptom networks. R1 "Bounce back quickly" (-3.342) was the core bridge symptom connecting the three network clusters. A comparison of male and female networks indicated that the overall network structure exhibited no significant sex differences; however, the global strength of the female network was significantly higher. The strongest positive associations remained consistent across the male and female networks (R1 "Bounce back quickly" and R3 "Recover from stress quickly"). A7 "Panic" emerged as a shared core symptom in both male and female networks.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: "Panic" was identified as the central symptom in the anxiety-depression-resilience symptom networks, while "Bounce back quickly" served as the key bridge node connecting these three symptom clusters. These findings provide potential symptom-level targets for future psychological assessments and intervention research. Additionally, there were significant differences in global strength between male and female networks, with gender-specific strategies recommended for each.

items.authors: Chen H, Zhang N, Feng Y, Tao M, Geng C.

sections.text: Depression is a common comorbidity in patients with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), suggesting potential epidemiological and pathophysiological connections between these two age-related chronic diseases. Extensive clinical evidence demonstrates that depression is closely associated with both the incidence and prognosis of HFpEF. sections.text: There is growing evidence on the positive effects of the arts and arts therapies for mental health (MH) outcomes. This review aims to fill a research gap by establishing the evidence on the effects of arts-based interventions on selected MH outcomes for children and young people (CYP).

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: Our systematic review and meta-analysis included randomised controlled trials with CYP aged 5-24 years receiving any type of arts-based intervention. items.title: Machine learning for early detection and mood shift prediction in bipolar disorder: a systematic review.
items.authors: Fang S, Chen S.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Bipolar Disorder (BD) is a serious mental illness characterized by recurrent episodes of mania and depression. Early detection and the prediction of shifts between mood states are critical for effective management and suicide prevention. Machine learning models analyzing data from clinical records, neuroimaging, and passive sensing (e.g., smartphones) are emerging as promising tools for this purpose.

sections.heading: Objective
sections.text: This systematic review evaluates the use of machine learning for the early detection of BD and the prediction of mood shifts, synthesizing evidence on different data modalities, algorithms, and predictive performance.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: A systematic search of PubMed, PsycINFO, and IEEE Xplore was conducted for studies published up to January 2026. We included original research articles that applied machine learning to data from individuals with BD for diagnosis/classification or prediction of mood episodes.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: A total of 37 studies met the inclusion criteria. For early detection (BD vs. HC or MDD), neuroimaging-based models achieved mean AUCs of 0.82-0.88. For mood shift prediction, digital phenotyping models using smartphone sensor data achieved AUCs of 0.75-0.85 for predicting manic or depressive episodes 1-2 weeks in advance.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: Machine learning shows significant promise for both early detection and mood shift prediction in BD. Multimodal approaches combining neuroimaging, clinical, and digital phenotyping data represent the most promising future direction. However, larger, prospective studies with external validation are needed before clinical implementation.

items.title: From Gendered Diagnosis to Community Care: How Borderline Personality Disorder Organizes Community Mental Health Nursing Practice.
items.authors: Galea R, Rodgers A, MacDonald C, Robertson A, Rooney A.

sections.text: Borderline personality disorder (BPD) is a contested diagnosis that has been criticized for pathologizing women's responses to trauma, adversity, and relational harm. This paper examines how BPD, as a gendered, historically situated, and institutionally mediated diagnostic category, shapes community mental health nursing (CMHN) practice. Using a critical conceptual analysis, it synthesizes historical, feminist, psychiatric, nursing, and Mad studies literature, combining genealogical, critical feminist, and social-structural perspectives. The paper argues that BPD functions not only as a clinical description of symptoms but also as an institutional category that influences documentation, referral pathways, eligibility criteria, and service design. Through these processes, the diagnosis shapes clinical visibility, therapeutic relationships, service access, and continuity of care. Moving beyond explanations of stigma that focus solely on individual clinician attitudes, the analysis demonstrates how diagnostic meanings are reproduced through organizational and health system structures, contributing to forms of structural stigma that constrain relational and trauma-informed care. The paper concludes with implications and recommendations for nursing practice, education, service delivery, and policy, including trauma-informed and relational approaches to assessment, non-stigmatizing documentation practices, transparent referral and eligibility processes, investment in community-based services, and strengthened clinical supervision and workforce supports.

items.title: Indirect moxibustion therapy improves insomnia and associated symptoms in patients with schizophrenia.
items.authors: Cai J, Wu M, Zhang J.

sections.heading: Objective
sections.text: To evaluate the efficacy of low-dose dexzopiclone combined with Indirect moxibustion (IM), compared with sham Indirect moxibustion (SIM), on sleep quality (PSQI) and quality of life (SQLS) in patients with schizophrenia and comorbid insomnia.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: This single-center randomized controlled trial (NCT06171308) obtained ethics approval from Shanghai Mental Health Center (SMHC-IRB-2023-08). A total of 120 participants were randomly assigned to the IM group (n = 60) or the SIM group (n = 60), receiving 8 weeks of standardized intervention.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Baseline PSQI and SQLS scores were comparable between the two groups. After 4 and 8 weeks, the IM group demonstrated significantly lower PSQI and SQLS scores than the SIM group (PSQI at week 4: 10.10 ± 1.76 vs. 13.50 ± 1.65, week 8: 10.65 ± 1.54 vs. 12.77 ± 2.05, SQLS at week 4: 28.78 ± 8.84 vs. 35.56 ± 3.38, week 8: 30.36 ± 10.63 vs. 38.07 ± 3.42). The improvement in the IM group was significantly greater than that in the SIM group in terms of change from baseline (PSQI: -3.399 [95% CI: -4.078 to -2.719] at week 4, -2.115 [95% CI: -2.795 to -1.435] at week 8, SQLS: -6.801 [95% CI: -9.104 to -4.462] at week 4, -7.732 [95% CI: -10.071 to -5.393] at week 8), with all adjusted intergroup differences being statistically significant (P < 0.001).

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: Adjunctive Indirect Moxibustion led to statistically significant and clinically meaningful improvements in sleep quality and quality of life compared to sham procedure in this patient population over an 8-week period. These preliminary findings suggest IM is a promising adjunctive therapy. Further multicenter, long-term trials with expanded outcome indicators are required to validate its generalizability and sustained efficacy.

items.title: Psychometric evaluation of the Persian version of the school-to-work transition anxiety scale in senior nursing students.
items.authors: Shahsavari H, Nadali J, Ghasempour S, Mirhosseini S, Sayadi L, Hashemi Ali Abadi S, Divani A.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Senior nursing students frequently encounter transition anxiety during internships, a phenomenon that adversely affects their mental health, academic performance, and the quality of patient care. Although Iran has introduced internship programs to reduce transition shock, their effectiveness remains unclear due to the lack of a validated Persian assessment tool. This study sought to evaluate the validity and reliability of the Persian adaptation of the school-to-work transition anxiety scale in nursing students.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: This methodological research was carried out to examine the structural validity and internal reliability of the scale, utilizing data gathered from October 2024 to May 2025. A total population sampling approach was used. All eligible final-year nursing students were identified using the official enrollment list maintained by the faculty's education office and were invited to participate. A total of 342 students participated and were divided into two independent samples: 171 participants for exploratory factor analysis (EFA) and 171 participants for confirmatory factor analysis (CFA). EFA, using the maximum likelihood extraction method with Promax rotation, was conducted to identify the latent factor structure. Subsequently, CFA was performed on the second independent sample to verify the proposed model. Convergent validity was assessed following the Fornell and Larcker approach by calculating the average variance extracted (AVE) and composite reliability (CR), while discriminant validity was evaluated using the Heterotrait-Monotrait (HTMT) ratio. Internal consistency was examined using Cronbach's alpha and McDonald's omega coefficients, and stability was assessed using the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC).

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: The study included 342 nursing students (55.85% male, mean age 22.81 ± 2.16 years, grade point average 16.83 ± 1.31). Qualitative face validity confirmed all items as clear, relevant, and important. Content validity was confirmed, with minor revisions to three items and the removal of five items (CVR > 0.56). EFA extracted four factors (58.71% variance), with two items removed due to low factor loadings. CFA supported model fit (χ²/DF = 1.665, RMSEA = 0.063, CFI = 0.917). Convergent validity was confirmed for "Interpersonal Interactions" and "Fear of Being Infected" factors based on AVE and CR values. Discriminant validity was confirmed, as all HTMT coefficients were below the 0.85 threshold. Internal consistency of all factors was confirmed by Cronbach's alpha and McDonald's omega values greater than 0.7, and the stability of the scale was confirmed by evaluation of the ICC with 0.75 acceptable threshold. The final Persian version comprised 24 items across the same four-factor structure as the original 31-item scale.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: The school-to-work transition anxiety scale demonstrated strong reliability and validity, confirming its suitability as a self-report instrument for assessing transition-related anxiety among final-year nursing students in Iran.

items.title: Performance and response time in emotion recognition and mentalizing measures in patients with schizophrenia.
items.authors: Ruiz-Toca A, Hernández-Gómez A, Andrade-González N, Fernández-Aragón C, Stiles BJ, Fernandez-Egea E, Rodriguez-Jimenez R, Lahera G.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Schizophrenia is associated with marked impairments in social cognition, particularly in emotion recognition and mentalizing. Although these deficits have been extensively documented, most studies rely on static, highly controlled measures and focus primarily on accuracy-based outcomes, thereby limiting ecological validity. This study aimed to examine performance and response times across static and dynamic social-cognitive measures in patients with schizophrenia compared to healthy controls, and to investigate the effects of speed instructions on emotion recognition performance.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: In a sample of patients with schizophrenia (n = 90) and matched healthy controls (n = 100), we evaluated social cognition through two validated measures: the Penn Emotion Recognition Test (ER-40) for emotion recognition and the Movie for the Assessment of Social Cognition (MASC) for mentalizing, respectively. Performance and response times were the main outcome variables.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Patients showed worse performance and longer response times than controls on the ER-40 and MASC measures. Across the entire sample, there was a statistically significant inverse association between response time and the rate of correct answers in both ER-40 and MASC measures. Speed instructions in the ER-40 did not influence performance or response times in either group. In the MASC, patients exhibited more mentalizing errors than controls. Additionally, patients identified anger more quickly than fear or sadness, a pattern not observed in the healthy control group.

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: Integrating accuracy and response time provides a comprehensive characterization of social-cognitive deficits in patients with schizophrenia. These findings highlight the importance of incorporating response time and dynamic measures to enhance the ecological validity of social-cognitive assessment and suggest that future rehabilitation programs may benefit from addressing both accuracy and response speed in emotion recognition and mentalizing domains.

items.title: Caring for the Caregivers: A Narrative Review of Physician Health Protection Across High-Income Countries and Lessons for Low- and Middle-Income Countries.
items.authors: Razaq HB, Saeed O, Reshtin M, Arshad MU, Usman W, Kashif N, Fawad Ul Hassan M, Sohail A, Khawaja AA, Irshad S, Mehmood Qadri H.

sections.text: Healthcare physicians (HCPs) across the world experience substantial mental, physical, and occupational health challenges, yet they remain an often-neglected group within healthcare systems. High levels of burnout, depression, anxiety, sleep disturbance, professional dissatisfaction, and even suicide have been reported in diverse settings, directly affecting patient safety and overall health system performance. This narrative review aimed to synthesize existing evidence on physician mental, physical, and professional health, with particular attention to similarities and differences between high-income countries (HICs) and low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). Peer-reviewed scientific articles, policy documents, and credible international reports examining physician well-being and workforce protection were analyzed. Recurrent themes across regions include burnout, depression, suicide risk, unsafe working conditions, professional dissatisfaction, migration, and collective actions such as strikes. In line with the objective of this review, the evidence also highlights important differences in how these challenges manifest and are addressed in HICs compared with LMICs. Although many of these problems are present globally, their severity is often greater in LMICs because of weaker occupational protections, limited access to mental health services, financial insecurity, and structural constraints within under-resourced health systems. The review therefore emphasizes that physician health should be viewed as a system-level and ethical responsibility rather than an individual failing. It further proposes practical and policy-oriented strategies that LMICs can adopt, such as confidential support pathways, regulatory reforms, and leadership accountability, to strengthen physician well-being without requiring major infrastructure expansion.

items.title: Central Auditory Processing Disorder in Children: A Multidisciplinary Approach.
items.authors: Alnoury MK, Ferre JM, Hemdi AJ, Abuzinadah H, Alnoury I, Alnoury KI.

sections.text: Central Auditory Processing Disorder (CAPD) is an impairment in the neural processing of sound information across the central auditory nerve system, not caused by peripheral hearing loss. The literature has highlighted the relationship between CAPD and learning difficulties and other conditions such as attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). This comprehensive review aims to describe a multidisciplinary clinical approach utilizing perspectives from otolaryngologists, audiologists, and psychologists. An expert panel of otolaryngologists, audiologists, and psychologists reviewed the literature and leveraged their clinical expertise to outline the multidisciplinary approach. The otolaryngologist's role is to comprehensively examine the patient's medical history and head and neck region to identify any potential causes of hearing loss, such as genetic or acquired factors. The audiologist conducts specialized tests specifically designed to assess central auditory processing abilities. Additionally, psychological assessment plays an important role in understanding the impact of cognitive and emotional factors on CAPD. The multidisciplinary approach detailed in this study will assist clinicians in establishing multidisciplinary clinics that would facilitate accurate diagnoses and provide personalized interventions, such as speech and language therapy and accommodations in academic settings.

items.title: Recurrent Cylindrical Battery Ingestion in Borderline Personality Disorder: Balancing Medical Risk and Behavioural Reinforcement.
items.authors: Monteiro C, Castro J, Macas R, Barbosa AS.

sections.text: Intentional foreign body ingestion is a recurrent and clinically challenging form of self-harm in patients with borderline personality disorder (BPD). Although medical guidance informs the management of individual ingestion events, recurrent presentations raise additional questions about the function of the behaviour and the consequences of repeated medical intervention. We report an 18-year-old patient with BPD and previously documented factitious features who had six episodes of intentional foreign body ingestion during a two-month psychiatric admission in 2026: five involving cylindrical batteries, including re-ingestion of a previously passed battery, and one involving a metal screw. Serial psychiatric assessments identified no psychotic symptoms. The behavioural context evolved from impulsive and reactive self-harm to later episodes that the patient described as retaliatory in the context of perceived interpersonal rejection. Multidisciplinary management integrated established medical indications with longitudinal psychiatric formulation. Endoscopic retrieval was undertaken when clinically indicated, whereas distally progressing batteries were managed conservatively with close clinical and radiological monitoring. No major medical complications occurred. This case illustrates a recurring dilemma at the interface between psychiatric and medical care: medically necessary procedures should never be withheld because of concerns about behavioural reinforcement, but unnecessary intervention may become incorporated into maladaptive behavioural and interpersonal patterns when a safe conservative alternative exists. Psychiatric formulation can therefore complement medical risk assessment and support consistent, proportionate multidisciplinary care.

items.title: Severe Malnutrition Revealing Psychotic Depression in an Elderly Patient Successfully Treated With Electroconvulsive Therapy: A Case Report.
items.authors: Sumya UM, Hamid T.

sections.text: Depression in older adults can sometimes present mainly with physical symptoms. This may delay recognition of the underlying psychiatric illness. We describe a 74‑year‑old man admitted to a medical ward with severe malnutrition caused by almost complete refusal of food. Extensive medical investigations did not reveal an organic cause. The patient was initially treated with antidepressant medication and nutritional support. However, his condition continued to deteriorate. A second psychiatric assessment identified severe psychotic depression with impaired decision‑making capacity and starvation syndrome. The patient was transferred urgently to a psychiatric unit and treated with bilateral electroconvulsive therapy (ECT). Following treatment, there was rapid improvement in mood, engagement, and oral intake. This case highlights the importance of reconsidering psychiatric diagnoses when medically unwell patients fail to improve and demonstrates the effectiveness of ECT in severe late‑life depression.

items.title: Altered Inhibitory Control Across Subclinical Depression and Major Depressive Disorder: Evidence From Stroop Tasks and Diffusion Modeling.
items.authors: Ye Q, Qiao YS, Jin JJ, Zhang SY, Li YD, Dou WJ, Jin K, Ni K, Yang Z, Li BM, Cai XL.

sections.text: Inhibitory control deficits are central to cognitive dysfunction in major depressive disorder (MDD), yet how such deficits vary across subclinical depression and MDD remains unclear. Childhood trauma may further contribute to variability in inhibitory control. This study examined behavioral and computational markers of inhibitory control across nonemotional and emotional contexts in healthy, subclinical depression, and MDD groups and explored associations with childhood trauma. Thirty individuals with subclinical depression, 33 patients with MDD, and 36 healthy controls (HCs) completed three Stroop tasks (color-word, emotion, and face-word), during which reaction times (RTs) were recorded. Latent cognitive parameters were estimated using the drift diffusion model (DDM) and diffusion model for conflict tasks (DMCs). Associations between these indicators and childhood trauma were examined. Patients with MDD showed significantly longer RTs than subclinical individuals in emotion and face-word Stroop tasks. Computational modeling revealed prolonged nondecision time in MDD, relative to subclinical depression (color-word Stroop task) and HCs (emotion Stroop task). In the subclinical group, greater childhood trauma was associated with faster RTs in incongruent face-word trials and shorter nondecision time in the color-word Stroop task. Our findings support a possible inverted U-shaped pattern of inhibitory control across depressive severity, with enhanced performance in subclinical depression but poorer performance in MDD. Enhanced inhibitory control in subclinical depression may reflect compensatory adaptation linked to early adversity. These findings provide novel insights into stage-related differences of inhibitory control in depression.

items.title: Depression, C-Reactive Protein, and the Risk of Mortality During Middle and Late Adulthood.
items.authors: Banerjee S, Khubchandani J, Beydoun MA, Nkemjika S, Batra K.

sections.text: Background and Purpose: Mental illnesses, including depression, are major contributors to disability and health loss globally. Research has increasingly focused on identifying biochemical markers, such as C-reactive protein (CRP), to better understand the link between systemic inflammation and psychiatric disorders. However, the long-term health impacts of their coexistence are underexplored. This study aimed to investigate the relationship between depression, elevated CRP levels, and mortality risk among community-dwelling older adults in the United States. Methods: Data from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) from 2005-2010 were utilized, linked with mortality data up to December 2019. The sample included 4606 adults aged 50 years and older. Depression was assessed through self-reported measures, and elevated CRP was defined as serum CRP ≥ 2 mg/L. Participants were categorized into four groups: depression only, elevated CRP only, both conditions, or neither. Cox regression models were employed to estimate hazard ratios (HRs) for all-cause and cardiovascular mortality, adjusting for sociodemographic and health-related covariates. Results: Individuals with both depression and elevated CRP had the highest risk of all-cause mortality (HR = 3.56, 95% CI = 1.41-8.97) and cardiovascular mortality (HR = 14.42, 95% CI = 4.29-21.06) compared to those with neither condition. Elevated CRP alone and depression alone were also independently associated with increased mortality risk. Predictors such as age, poverty, smoking, obesity, diabetes, and cardiovascular history significantly influenced these associations. Conclusion: The coexistence of depression and systemic inflammation markedly elevates the risk of mortality. These findings highlight the need for integrated clinical strategies targeting both mental health and inflammation to mitigate mortality risks in vulnerable populations.

items.title: Profiles of Cognitive Appraisal of Non-Suicidal Self-Injury Scars and Their Clinical Correlates in Adults with a History of Self-Injury: A Cross-Sectional Study.
items.authors: Grigoreva AA, Fedotov IA, Marachev MP, Kondratovich AK.
items.journal: European journal of investigation in health, psychology and education
items.journal_abbrev: Eur J Investig Health Psychol Educ

sections.text: Scars are the most durable consequence of non-suicidal self-injury (NSSI), but how patients appraise them, and how appraisal dimensions combine within individuals, remains unclear. In this cross-sectional study, 234 adults with a history of NSSI and at least one scar, recruited consecutively in Ryazan and Moscow, Russia, completed the Russian NSSI Scar Cognition Scale (Hopelessness, Shame, Inner Strength) and measures of suicidal ideation, social anxiety, rumination, body-image dysphoria and NSSI functions. Profiles were derived by cluster analysis and tested for stability. Three stable profiles emerged: low-salience (55.1%), negative-dominant (28.2%) and strength-dominant (16.7%). The negative-dominant profile showed the highest suicidal ideation, social anxiety, rumination, body-image dysphoria and self-punishment; the strength-dominant profile showed suicidal ideation and social anxiety similar to the low-salience profile, intermediate rumination and body-image dysphoria, and the strongest endorsement of NSSI functions. These differences persisted after covariate adjustment. Scar appraisal explained a further 7.9% of variance in suicidal ideation beyond demographics, self-injury status and general distress; scar visibility explained none. In behavioural remission, the negative-dominant profile reported higher suicidal ideation than the other profiles. Scar appraisal distinguishes subgroups with different clinical correlates. Longitudinal studies are needed to establish whether these profiles predict outcomes or can guide treatment.

items.title: Psychological Distress and Resources Under Prolonged Exposure to an Environmental Threat: A Qualitative Study on Inhabitants Exposed to the Campi Flegrei 's Bradyseism.
items.authors: Sarrecchia A, Ludovico N, Milani A, Chiozza V, Bonaiuto M.
items.journal: European journal of investigation in health, psychology and education
items.journal_abbrev: Eur J Investig Health Psychol Educ

sections.text: Prolonged environmental threats expose communities to recurring hazard cues and uncertainty, yet psychological consequences and resources involved in adaptation remain underexplored. This study examined psychological outcomes, personal and social resources, and their co-occurrence among inhabitants exposed to bradyseism in Campi Flegrei, southern Italy. Fifty-two semi-structured interviews were conducted with inhabitants of the Campi Flegrei area. Eighteen were recruited without reference to a specific stakeholder role, whereas 34 were recruited based on their institutional, professional, or community roles. Narratives were examined through theory-driven thematic analysis. Six psychological outcomes were considered, including five distress-related negative psychological outcomes (i.e., anxiety, post-traumatic symptoms, depression, sleep disturbances, and suicidal ideation) and one adaptive psychological outcome (i.e., post-traumatic growth). Distress was classified using literature-derived categories, while the Social-psychological Antecedents to Resilience for Adaptation (SARA) classified resources by locus, specificity, and availability. Anxiety-related experiences were most frequent, followed by post-traumatic stress-related experiences, depression-related experiences, and sleep disturbances; post-traumatic growth was rare, and no segments related to suicidal ideation were identified. Risk perception, experience, acceptance, cognitive reappraisal, and place attachment were frequently identified as available resources in narratives involving distress, whereas information emerged predominantly as unavailable and available social support was identified only once in the corpus. These resources co-occurred with manifestations of distress without revealing a consistent protective pattern. The findings document the coexistence of resources and distress without establishing the direction of their relationships or a protective role. Future research should clarify resource-distress directionality and examine whether perceived agency explains why some resource constellations coexist with persistent distress, whereas others are associated with more adaptive responses under prolonged environmental threat.

items.title: Psychological Inflexibility and Suicidal Ideation in Pregnant Women: A Cross-Sectional Multiple Mediation Analysis of Depressive Symptoms, Insomnia, and Generalized Anxiety.
items.authors: Baños-Chaparro J, Artica-Martinez J, Caycho-Rodríguez T.
items.journal: European journal of investigation in health, psychology and education
items.journal_abbrev: Eur J Investig Health Psychol Educ

sections.text: Introduction: Suicidal ideation during pregnancy is an important public health concern. Psychological inflexibility may be associated with emotional and sleep-related symptoms linked to suicidal ideation; however, these patterns of association remain insufficiently understood in pregnant women. Objective: The objective was to examine the relationship between psychological inflexibility and suicidal ideation in pregnant women by evaluating the multiple mediating roles of depressive symptoms, insomnia, and generalized anxiety. Method: A quantitative, cross-sectional associative study using latent variables was conducted with 962 pregnant women receiving care at the National Maternal and Perinatal Institute (INMP), located in Cercado de Lima, Lima, Peru, between October and December 2025. Participants completed the Acceptance and Action Questionnaire-II (AAQ-II), Frequency of Suicidal Ideation Inventory (FSII), Athens Insomnia Scale (AIS), Patient Health Questionnaire-2 (PHQ-2), and Generalized Anxiety Disorder-2 (GAD-2). Structural equation modeling (SEM) was performed using R version 4.5.1 within the RStudio Version 4.5.1 environment. Results: The proposed model showed a good fit, scaled χ^2(179) = 506.334, p < 0.001, robust CFI = 0.968, robust TLI = 0.963, robust RMSEA = 0.052, 90% CI [0.046, 0.057], and SRMR = 0.030. Psychological inflexibility showed a significant direct association with suicidal ideation (β = 0.246, p < 0.001) and significant indirect associations through depressive symptoms (β = 0.245, p < 0.001) and insomnia (β = 0.030, p = 0.007), whereas the indirect association through generalized anxiety was not significant (β = 0.007, p = 0.749). The total indirect association was significant (β = 0.282, p < 0.001), while the direct association remained statistically significant after inclusion of the mediators. Conclusions: Psychological inflexibility was associated with suicidal ideation among pregnant women, with depressive symptoms and insomnia showing significant indirect associations. These cross-sectional findings identify relevant correlates of suicidal ideation that warrant further longitudinal investigation.

items.title: Suicide mortality and suicide method trends in the Region of the Americas, 2015-2021: a population-based time-series analysis of progress toward a one-third reduction target.
items.authors: Lange S, Martinez R, Guo K, Hennis AJM, Oliveria E Souza R.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: The suicide mortality rate is a key global indicator for monitoring progress toward improved mental health and well-being under the Sustainable Development Goals, and the World Health Organization Comprehensive Mental Health Action Plan has set an explicit suicide-specific target of reducing the age-standardized suicide mortality rate by one-third by 2030 (with a baseline year of 2015). This study assessed temporal trends in suicide mortality and suicide methods in the Region of the Americas using average annual percent change (AAPC) for the period 2015-2021.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: Age-standardized and age group-specific suicide mortality rates (per 100,000 population) for the region, subregions, and by country for 2000-2021, and proportion of suicides by method by country, overall and by sex for 2015-2021, were obtained from the World Health Organization Global Health Estimates and the Pan American Health Organization Regional Mortality Database, respectively. In this population-based time-series analysis, AAPC was estimated using joinpoint regression analyses. The AAPCs for suicide mortality rates between 2015 and 2021 were compared with the compound annual reduction required to achieve a one-third reduction by 2030 (-2·67%).

sections.heading: Findings
sections.text: The regional age-standardized suicide mortality rate increased by 1·05% (95% CI: 0·85%, 1·26%; p ≤ 0·0001) annually on average between 2015 and 2021, driven by males (AAPC: 0·99%, 95% CI: 0·81%, 1·17%; p ≤ 0·0001), as the rate among females remained relatively stable during this period (AAPC: 0·02%, 95% CI: -1·38%, 1·45%; p = 0·97). Only 10 countries (30·3%; out of 33) showed significant declines exceeding the 2·67% annual reduction needed to achieve the one-third reduction target by 2030. Across countries, the distribution of recorded suicide methods shifted over time, with increases in the proportion of suicides involving hanging and decreases in the proportions involving firearms and poisoning.

sections.heading: Interpretation
sections.text: Suicide mortality in the region is rising, and the target of a one-third reduction by 2030 is unlikely to be met regionally; however, progress varies considerably across countries, with 10 (30·3%) making substantial progress toward the target. Urgent, coordinated action is needed in the countries with high and increasing suicide mortality rates, combining evidence-based means restriction strategies with broader upstream interventions that address social, economic and health-system determinants of suicide risk.

items.title: Alteration of empathy-related behaviors in two strains of mice expressing mutations of the α5 cholinergic nicotinic receptor subunit.
items.authors: Tochon L, Pagèze C, Henkous N, Guillou JL, David V.

sections.text: A single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) of the alpha5 subunit of nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChRs) increases human risk for nicotine dependence, alcohol use disorders (AUDs), and schizophrenia. items.title: Cariprazine Augmentation and Sustained Remission of Physical Aggression in Clozapine-Treated Treatment-Resistant Schizophrenia: A Case Report.
items.authors: Leijala J, Mustonen A.

sections.text: Persistent aggression may occur in treatment-resistant schizophrenia (TRS) despite long-term clozapine treatment and multiple augmentation strategies. We describe a male patient in his sixties with a decades-long history of schizophrenia who required prolonged psychiatric inpatient care because of recurrent, unpredictable physical assaults toward other patients, staff, relatives, and police. This included treatment at a state forensic psychiatric hospital because of treatment complexity and safety concerns, not forensic legal status. Aggression persisted during adequately monitored high-dose clozapine treatment and several augmentation strategies. The last documented physical assault occurred in October 2021. Cariprazine 1.5 mg/day was initiated in November 2021, primarily for longstanding negative symptoms. Within approximately seven weeks, mood and participation in communal ward activities improved. No further physical assaults were documented during more than 4 years of follow-up. The patient subsequently transitioned to voluntary treatment and supported housing. Later somatic illnesses, temporary interruptions of oral medication, and substantial fluctuations in clozapine serum concentrations were not followed by renewed physical aggression. This case describes a prolonged temporal association between cariprazine augmentation and the absence of recurrent physical assaults, but the single-case design, episodic pretreatment course, concomitant treatment changes, and absence of standardized ratings preclude causal inference.

items.title: Latent Profiles of Primary Emotional Systems and Their Associations with PTSD, CPTSD, Attachment, and Childhood Adversity.
items.authors: Ferrajão P, Rocha RF, Martins AQ.
items.journal: European journal of investigation in health, psychology and education
items.journal_abbrev: Eur J Investig Health Psychol Educ

sections.text: Adverse childhood experiences are associated with trauma-related psychopathology, but individual differences in affective organization may contribute to heterogeneous outcomes. This study aimed to identify latent profiles of primary emotional systems and examine their associations with attachment, childhood maltreatment, and posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and complex PTSD (CPTSD). A community sample of 917 Portuguese adults completed measures of primary emotional systems, adult attachment, childhood maltreatment, and PTSD/CPTSD symptoms. Latent profile analyses were conducted separately for women and men, followed by measurement invariance testing and multinomial logistic regression analyses. Four profiles were identified in both sexes: Negative Affect, Low Affective Activation, Balanced Affective Functioning, and Positive Affect. Partial measurement invariance indicated sex-related differences in ANGER, FEAR, and PANIC, while the overall profile structure was comparable across sexes. Negative Affect was associated with PTSD, CPTSD, and fearful attachment in both sexes. Low Affective Activation was associated with CPTSD and dismissing attachment, with additional associations varying by sex. The findings indicate that primary emotional systems form heterogeneous configurations that are differentially associated with developmental, interpersonal, and clinical characteristics. Person-centered assessment may complement symptom-based approaches, although causal inference and profile stability cannot be established.

items.title: The Sequential Roles of Psychological Flexibility and Positivity in the Association Between Post-Traumatic Stress Symptoms and Depressive Symptoms Among Earthquake Survivors in Türkiye.
items.authors: Peker A, Cengiz S, Eroğlu Y, Laranjeira C, Yıldırım M.
items.journal: European journal of investigation in health, psychology and education
items.journal_abbrev: Eur J Investig Health Psychol Educ

sections.text: Earthquakes can have substantial consequences for psychological well-being, including post-traumatic stress and depressive symptoms. Drawing on Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT), which conceptualizes psychological flexibility as a central process in adaptive psychological functioning, this study examined the sequential mediating roles of psychological flexibility and positivity in the association between post-traumatic stress symptoms and depressive symptoms among survivors of the two major earthquakes that struck Türkiye on 6 February 2023. This cross-sectional study included 834 earthquake survivors ( M age = 26.7; 71.1% female) who were assessed approximately three months after the earthquakes. Participants completed validated self-report measures of post-traumatic stress symptoms, psychological flexibility, positivity, and depressive symptoms. Depressive symptoms were assessed using the 12-item depression subscale of the Brief Symptom Inventory and were analyzed as a continuous variable. Correlation and sequential mediation analyses were conducted, with indirect effects evaluated using bootstrapping. Post-traumatic stress symptoms were positively associated with depressive symptoms and negatively associated with psychological flexibility and positivity. Psychological flexibility was positively associated with positivity and negatively associated with depressive symptoms, while positivity was negatively associated with depressive symptoms. Sequential mediation analysis indicated that psychological flexibility and positivity mediated the association between post-traumatic stress symptoms and depressive symptoms. These findings suggest that psychological flexibility and positivity may represent relevant psychological processes in the association between post-traumatic stress and depressive symptoms among earthquake survivors and may inform post-disaster psychological support.

items.title: State Policies and Clinicians' Perspectives on the Inclusion of Medical Cannabis in the Prescription Drug Monitoring Program.
items.authors: Gregor CM, Tian MY, Tusing LD, Wright EA, Piper BJ, Romagnoli KM.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: Studies have shown that information on cannabis use remains almost absent from electronic health records (EHRs). The Prescription Drug Monitoring Program (PDMP) is utilized by some states to capture medical cannabis (MC) use information. We assessed clinicians' and administrators' perceptions of incorporating MC use information into PDMPs and described current state-level practices for MC inclusion.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: The primary aim was to identify characteristics that influence cannabis documentation throughout the EHR, while this exploratory analysis addressed the value of the PDMP for MC use information. In this mixed-methods study, we conducted 50 qualitative interviews with clinicians and administrators in March-July 2023 assessing MC in PDMPs and a national survey sent to 51 state PDMP administrators examining MC information shared with clinicians.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Of the 50 participants interviewed, 24 were explicitly asked about the PDMP, and four additional participants organically mentioned the PDMP or similar program and discussed its impact. Among the 28 participants, 19 (67.9%) believed MC in the PDMP would positively impact patient care. Fifty states and the District of Columbia responded to our survey. Six states (Connecticut, Louisiana, New York, Ohio, Mississippi, and Virginia) included MC dispensing. Four states (Arizona, Illinois, North Dakota, and Utah) have an MC card indicator in the PDMP.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: Patients and clinicians could benefit from MC in the PDMPs; access to clinically actionable information could prevent drug/drug interactions, cannabis-induced psychosis, and enable early intervention for misuse. Since the USA changed MC to schedule III, policymakers may consider these findings.

items.title: Sex-dependent cross-resilience to social defeat and learned helplessness: The role of BDNF-ERK signaling and norepinephrine.
items.authors: Bairachnaya M, Penney L, Fakhfouri G, Isingrini E, Giros B.

sections.text: Major depressive disorder (MDD) and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) are two of the most prevalent and disabling psychiatric conditions, both closely tied to stress exposure. While they have distinct diagnostic criteria, MDD and PTSD share considerable comorbidity, overlapping behavioral symptoms, and common neurobiological pathways. However, not all individuals exposed to chronic or traumatic stress develop these disorders, highlighting the importance of resilience, the capacity to maintain psychological and physiological stability under stress. An emerging yet incompletely understood aspect of stress adaptation is cross-resilience, defined as the extent to which resilience or susceptibility to one form of stress generalizes to subsequent stressors across contexts. While animal models have effectively captured individual differences in stress responses, few have explored whether resilience generalizes across distinct stress modalities or differs by sex. We examined cross-resilience using two validated rodent models: chronic social defeat stress (CSDS) and learned helplessness (LH). These paradigms model complementary aspects of stress vulnerability. We assessed how prior CSDS experience influenced subsequent responses to LH. We also evaluated the role of the noradrenergic system using wild-type and norepinephrine (NE)-deficient (VMAT2^loxDBHcre KO) mice. Behavioral phenotyping was combined with molecular analyses in key brain regions involved in emotion, motivation, and fear processing: the ventral tegmental area (VTA), nucleus accumbens (NAc), and amygdala (AMY). We focused on BDNF and ERK/MAPK signaling pathways, known to mediate neuroplasticity and stress resilience. Our findings reveal sex-specific patterns of cross-resilience, with prior CSDS resilience predicting LH resilience in males but not females. Molecular results indicate distinct adaptations across brain regions and sexes, underscoring the biological complexity of resilience. These insights may inform personalized strategies for preventing and treating stress-related disorders.

items.title: A tool to evaluate the impact of lived experience involvement in research: the Brain and Genomics Hub Impact Log protocol.
items.authors: Gergel T, Wright T, Geshica L, Vicary E, Kennett J, Delgaram-Nejad O, Edwards C, Ganesh HVS, Kabir T, Harrison CL, Heard J, Dash G, Bresner C, Jones I, Hall J, John A, Harrison NA, Walters JTR, Legge SE.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Despite widespread recognition of the value of lived experience involvement (LEI) in healthcare research and increased LE involvement activity, we lack established implementation methods and instruments for reporting and evaluating impact. We present a protocol for an innovative LE-led Impact Log tool and LEI framework, which may help to address some fundamental barriers to LEI. The Impact Log will be implemented within a five-year multidisciplinary transdiagnostic research project on severe mental illness and is also designed for wider adaptation and use. We include a short literature review on LEI impact, to provide in-depth background.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: The Impact Log framework is designed to integrate inclusive impactful LEI throughout all research stages, and to use a short accessible form to record and evaluate impact across three domains: design and delivery; interpersonal and environmental aspects; systems and processes. Impact Log tool and LEI design and implementation is led by LE study leads and specialist LE advisory panel, with combined research experience and LE, fully integrated within the wider research team. All Hub research participants will be offered accessible opportunities for remunerated lived experience input, and there will be outreach to ensure diverse representation, aided by the Hub's charity partners. Data collection and analysis will be LE led and will include iterative analysis to inform continuing development. Diverse formal and informal dissemination throughout the project will maximise wider stakeholder engagement.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: The potential value of this research is to implement a novel tool and framework for facilitating, recording and evaluating LEI in complex mental health research, which can be adapted for wider use. Strengths in design are LE leadership and cross-cutting LE research integration, incorporation of multiple domains, and a focus on facilitating diversity and inclusion within LEI. Potential limitations for this project and wider adaptation may include limited resources, risk of bias and health challenges.

items.title: Prefrontal dysfunction and impulsive decision-making in female methamphetamine use disorder: a fNIRS study.
items.authors: Zhang H, Ou S, Hu Y, Yuan C, Zou Q, Zhang H, Lei P.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Heightened preference for immediate over delayed rewards is a well-established feature of substance use disorders, yet the neural basis of this tendency in women with methamphetamine use disorder (MUD) remains insufficiently characterized. Delay discounting provides a useful behavioral index of impulsive decision-making, and convergent evidence implicates prefrontal valuation and control systems in addiction-related choice abnormalities.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: Twenty-five women with MUD and 25 healthy women completed an intertemporal decision-making task under gain and loss frames. Delay discounting rates were estimated using the hyperbolic discounting parameter (k). Functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) was used to assess oxygenated hemoglobin (HbO) responses in predefined prefrontal regions of interest, with a focus on the medial orbitofrontal cortex (mOFC) and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC). Trait impulsivity/reinforcement sensitivity was assessed using the BIS/BAS scales. Behavioral discounting was analyzed using a linear mixed model, and neural indices were analyzed using repeated-measures ANCOVAs with age as a covariate and FDR correction across ROIs.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Compared with healthy controls, women with MUD showed significantly steeper delay discounting, indicating a stronger preference for immediate outcomes. They also exhibited lower HbO responses in the right mOFC and left DLPFC during task performance, as well as reduced task-related HbO change in the right DLPFC. Lower right mOFC mean task-window HbO was associated with higher BIS/BAS composite scores. No robust Group × Frame interaction was observed for behavioral discounting.

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: Women with MUD showed altered intertemporal choice and reduced prefrontal hemodynamic responses in regions implicated in value evaluation and cognitive control. These findings support the relevance of prefrontal dysfunction to impulsive decision-making in female MUD while also indicating that framing-related effects should be interpreted cautiously. The study extends the limited literature on women with MUD and supports the use of fNIRS to examine prefrontal mechanisms of addiction-related decision-making.

items.title: Expert guidance to inform coordinated suicide postvention responses: A Delphi study.
items.authors: Reifels L, Fraser T, Asche A, Bekerman M, Sutton M, Flynn L, Bottern S, Humphries R, Whyte M, Andriessen K.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: The impact of suicide is profound for affected individuals, families and communities. Suicide postvention responses, inclusive of bereavement support, have been recognised as having made a valuable contribution to suicide prevention efforts. Postvention Protocol Response Groups (PPRGs) have emerged as a central mechanism to facilitate a coordinated service system response following a suspected suicide, mobilising a range of local services to provide early intervention support to bereaved communities across a defined geographical area. There is an important role to be played by these key agencies, support services, and community groups in responding to these impacts. However, little is known about the effective implementation of PPRGs.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: We used the Delphi method to obtain expert consensus regarding best practice implementation of PPRGs. The two-round online Delphi survey involved a panel of 30 Australian experts (comprising past or present PPRG members, postvention experts, and response beneficiaries) who rated statements in terms of their importance for PPRG implementation.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: The 126 statements endorsed by 80% or more of panel members as "essential" or "important" regarding PPRG implementation covered key aspects of stakeholder engagement, governance, practice principles, operational aspects, data surveillance, preventative capacity, sustainability, and special considerations in rural areas. Expert recommendations will serve as the foundation for the development of a PPRG implementation guide.

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: This study provides valuable expert guidance and practice-based evidence to inform the establishment of PPRGs in areas of need, enhance the effectiveness and sustainability of existing PPRGs, and strengthen the implementation of localised postvention responses.
