items.title: Baum Test as an Adjunctive Monitoring Tool in a Case of Major Depressive Disorder With Prominent Anhedonia.
items.authors: Maekubo K, Maruta J.

sections.text: Anhedonia is a core symptom of major depressive disorder associated with poor prognosis and treatment resistance. Assessment often relies on subjective self-reports and clinician-rated scales, and discrepancies between these evaluations can complicate clinical interpretations. The Baum test, a projective tree-drawing test, has recently been examined using quantitative indices such as the number of occupied areas on a page, to allow a more objective assessment. Here, we report the case of a 58-year-old woman with major depressive disorder characterized by prominent anhedonia. Upon admission, evaluations demonstrated a marked discrepancy between the patient's self-rated depression score, which indicated moderate to severe symptoms, and the clinician-rated scale, which suggested only mild depression. During electroconvulsive therapy, the Baum test was repeatedly administered, and the number of occupied areas appeared to change in parallel with clinical improvement and subsequent symptom fluctuations. These findings suggest that the quantitative indices of the Baum test may reflect changes in motivational or behavioral engagement that are not fully captured by conventional rating scales. These findings serve as a hypothesis-generating observation suggesting that the Baum test may serve as a simple, noninvasive adjunctive tool for longitudinal symptom monitoring, though its interpretation should consider cognitive influences and future studies are needed to establish its diagnostic validity.

items.title: Mental Well-Being Among Emerging Adults With and Without SLD/ADHD During War.
items.authors: Alon R, Harel-Gadassi A.
items.journal: European journal of investigation in health, psychology and education
items.journal_abbrev: Eur J Investig Health Psychol Educ

sections.text: Emerging adulthood is marked by increasing independence and responsibility across educational, occupational, and social domains. During wartime, disruptions to daily routines, security, and perceived control may threaten mental well-being, understood as positive emotional, social, and psychological functioning. These challenges may be particularly salient for individuals with specific learning disabilities (SLD) and/or attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), who may experience difficulties in executive functioning and maintaining everyday routines. This study examined differences in mental well-being between emerging adults with and without SLD and/or ADHD and assessed the contributions of executive functioning, health-promoting daily activities, psychological capital, and perceived social support during wartime. Participants were 317 Israeli emerging adults aged 18-28 years. Among the 316 participants with valid diagnostic-group classification, 115 reported SLD and/or ADHD and 201 reported neither condition. Emerging adults with SLD and/or ADHD reported lower mental well-being, greater executive functioning difficulties, and lower engagement in health-promoting daily activities than those without SLD and/or ADHD. Mental well-being was positively associated with psychological capital, health-promoting daily activities, and perceived social support, and negatively associated with executive functioning difficulties. In the hierarchical regression, diagnostic-group status was initially associated with mental well-being but was no longer significant after psychological capital, health-promoting daily activities and executive functioning were entered; perceived social support made a small additional contribution. The final model explained 37.2% of the variance in mental well-being. These findings highlight the relevance of cognitive-functional, psychological, occupational, and social factors to mental well-being during a prolonged national crisis.

items.title: Dynamic dopamine signaling, prediction error, and microcircuit mechanisms in stress-induced depression-like behaviors.
items.authors: Mahmud A, Efremov L.
items.journal: Frontiers in cell and developmental biology

sections.text: Chronic stress contributes to major depressive disorder (MDD) phenotypes by disrupting coordinated neuromodulatory systems and their corresponding computational frameworks. In this review, we explore how the dynamic interplay of ventral tegmental area dopamine (DA) signaling, microcircuit gating, and prediction error mechanics orchestrates stress-induced depressive behaviors, such as anhedonia and amotivation. Rather than acting as the sole driver of depression, pathway-specific neuroadaptations across mesolimbic ( VTA→NAc ) and mesocortical ( VTA→PFC ) dopaminergic projections operate within a broader multi-transmitter landscape, interacting with serotonergic, noradrenergic, cholinergic, and glutamatergic/GABAergic systems. These signaling anomalies often translate into computational deficits in reinforcement learning, manifesting as blunted striatal reward prediction error (RPE) signals that scale directly with anhedonia severity. Chronic stress also disrupts cortical microcircuit gating governed by dopamine D1 and D2 receptors, inducing cellular senescence and collapsing ensemble synchrony within the prefrontal cortex and interconnected networks. Furthermore, specialized subcortical loops, including inputs from the nucleus accumbens (NAc), ventral hippocampus (vHIPP), lateral habenula (LHb), and locus coeruleus (LC), recalibrate overall susceptibility versus resilience by altering DA firing dynamics and population activity pools, often in a sex-specific manner. By bridging synaptic dopamine dynamics, subcortical prediction errors, and cortical ensemble synchrony, we propose a unified, multi-level framework demonstrating how stress-induced depressive behaviors result from a progressive breakdown in the brain's predictive coding and adaptive coping networks.

items.title: Health Behaviour Change in Weight Management for People With Higher Weight and Symptoms of Common Mental Health Problems: A Qualitative Study.
items.authors: Rysinova V, Brown S, Stock NM.
items.journal: Health expectations : an international journal of public participation in health care and health policy

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Adults with higher weight experience disproportionate rates of common mental health problems (CMHPs), including depression, anxiety and post-traumatic stress disorder. Tier 2 Weight Management Services (T2WMS) in the United Kingdom emphasise diet and physical activity with limited psychological input. Evidence on how people with co-occurring CMHPs symptoms experience health behaviour change within these programmes remains limited.

sections.heading: Objective
sections.text: To explore how adults with higher weight and symptoms of CMHPs engage with health behaviour change in T2WMS, incorporating service user and practitioner perspectives, and to identify barriers, facilitators and service implications.

sections.heading: Design
sections.text: Qualitative study using semi-structured interviews.

sections.heading: Setting and participants
sections.text: Service users (n = 11) and healthcare professionals (n = 11) recruited from UK T2WMS.

sections.heading: Main variables studied
sections.text: Barriers and facilitators to eating behaviours, physical activity, emotion regulation and self-regulation behaviours.

sections.heading: Main outcome measures
sections.text: Thematic patterns were analysed using codebook thematic analysis within a critical realist frame, with deductive mapping to the COM-B model and Theoretical Domains Framework (TDF).

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Five themes captured a dynamic interplay of emotional, social and structural factors: (1) The emotional weight of change, (2) Health on the margins of daily life, (3) Connection and judgement shape the journey, (4) Treating the whole person, and (5) Self-care as a foundation for lifelong change. Barriers to health behaviour change included emotional fluctuation, stigma, low self-efficacy, relational pressures and structural constraints. Facilitators included self-compassion, emotional regulation, small achievable goals, inclusive groups and supportive practitioner relationships.

sections.heading: Discussion and conclusions
sections.text: Provision centred on weight loss as the primary measure of success, delivered in a standardised format, was poorly aligned with the needs of those with symptoms of CMHPs. Embedding trauma sensitivity, relational safety, flexible pacing and broader outcome measures may better support sustained engagement. Mapping to COM-B/TDF and Behaviour Change Wheel intervention functions offers a psychologically informed framework to guide commissioners and practitioners.

sections.heading: Patient or public contribution
sections.text: An advisory group of four members (two with lived experience of higher weight and symptoms of CMHPs, two healthcare professionals delivering T2WMS) contributed to study design, recruitment materials and interview guides shaping the study's non-stigmatising terminology. All research participants were also invited to review preliminary findings, which informed refinements to thematic language. Patient and public involvement was documented using the GRIPP2 short-form framework.

items.title: Psychometric Evaluation of Sinhala and Tamil Measures of Suicidal Behavior and Interpersonal Suicide Risk Constructs in Sri Lanka.
items.authors: Baminiwatta A, Williams S, Rajapakse T, Gadambanathan T, Robinson J.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Valid and culturally appropriate instruments are essential for suicide research and risk screening. This study evaluated the psychometric properties of the Sinhala and Tamil versions of the Suicide Behaviors Questionnaire-Revised (SBQ-R), Interpersonal Needs Questionnaire-10 (INQ-10), and Acquired Capability for Suicide Scale-Fearlessness About Death (ACSS-FAD), which assess constructs of the Interpersonal Theory of Suicide (IPTS).

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: In this cross-sectional study, 551 university students (409 Sinhala-speaking, 142 Tamil-speaking) and 98 patients presenting with self-harm completed the measures. Structural validity, reliability, convergent validity, known-group validity, measurement invariance, and receiver operating characteristic analyses were performed.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: The SBQ-R demonstrated a unidimensional structure, good internal consistency (ordinal α = 0.86-0.92), language and gender invariance, and satisfactory convergent and known-group validity. The original seven-item ACSS-FAD performed poorly, whereas a four-item version demonstrated satisfactory psychometric properties. INQ-10 did not support the hypothesized two-factor structure, with relatively better support for a bifactor model. The SBQ-R discriminated between students and patients presenting with self-harm (AUC = 0.716, 95% CI = 0.656-0.777), with improved discrimination among patients reporting suicidal intent (AUC = 0.876, 95% CI = 0.820-0.931). The established cut-off of ≥7 was supported.

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: The Sinhala and Tamil SBQ-R demonstrated good psychometric properties and are suitable for suicide research and risk screening in Sri Lanka. The four-item ACSS-FAD appears preferable to the original version, whereas INQ-10 subscale scores should be interpreted cautiously. These findings support further research on suicidal behavior and evaluation of IPTS-based hypotheses in clinical and community populations in Sri Lanka.

items.title: Dyadic discrimination and mental well-being among older Americans.
items.authors: Stokes JE, Farmer HR.

sections.heading: Background and objectives
sections.text: There is a thorough literature on the mental health consequences of discrimination exposure in adulthood, yet little work to date has situated such experiences within a relational, dyadic context. The present brief report analyzes 2-wave longitudinal data from the Health and Retirement Study (2018-2022) to determine whether individuals' own or their intimate partner's experiences of discrimination were associated with changes to anxiety symptoms, perceived stress, and/or self-esteem over a 4-year period.

sections.heading: Research methods and design
sections.text: Dyadic lagged dependent variable models were estimated using a structural equation modeling framework with full information maximum likelihood methods to address missing data. A total of 1,484 individuals from 742 opposite-gender couples participated at both the 2018 and 2022 waves of data collection and comprised the analytic sample for this study.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Individuals' own exposure to everyday discrimination was associated with increased symptoms of anxiety and perceived stress, as well as with reduced self-esteem, over the 4-year period. A dyadic partner's exposure to everyday discrimination was associated with increased anxiety symptoms for men only, though post-hoc Wald tests failed to find a significant gender difference in effects.

sections.heading: Discussion and implications
sections.text: Discrimination is a chronic psychosocial stressor with harmful consequences for mental health of affected individuals even in mid and later life. Moreover, limited evidence suggests that discrimination may have dyadic consequences as well, though these patterns are mixed. Future research is needed to determine interpersonal mechanisms for the findings of interest.

items.title: Swedish Consensus Recommendation for Follow-Up After ICU Stay.
items.authors: Åkerman E, Schandl A, Ringdal M, Dahl O, Orwelius L.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: A substantial proportion of intensive care unit (ICU) survivors experience long-term physical, psychological and cognitive impairments after critical illness. However, methods for identifying patients in need of post-ICU support vary widely. As a result, many patients are left without access to established rehabilitation pathways. This consensus recommendation provides a framework for the organisation and content of follow-up for adult ICU survivors in Sweden, informed by available evidence, stakeholder perspectives and expert consensus.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: The National System for Knowledge-Driven Healthcare Management (NPO) in Sweden commissioned the development of a practice recommendation for the follow-up of critically ill adults. Multidisciplinary experts in ICU survivorship formed a task force group. A systematic literature search in four databases was conducted in 2024 to identify pre-existing systematic reviews on the topic. The literature was reviewed, assessed for quality and recommendations were developed based on the literature evidence. The draft was discussed among multiprofessional groups involved in follow-up, in workshops with critical care nurses (n = 30) and professionals responsible for follow-up clinics (n = 74) and among patient representatives (n = 4). The final draft underwent external peer review by representatives from relevant professional organisations, the national registry for intensive care and governmental agencies in Sweden.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: The consensus recommendation suggests that all adult patients with an ICU length of stay ≥ 48 h are recommended for follow-up, with an initial contact within 1 week of ICU discharge to assess clinical status, identify early problems and ensure continuity of care. Patients and their families are recommended to be offered an outpatient follow-up visit at 2-3 months after discharge, led by ICU clinicians and, when possible, delivered by a multidisciplinary team. Validated screening tools and objective tests are recommended to assess relevant outcomes, including post-traumatic stress, anxiety, depression, cognitive impairment, physical function and Health-Related Quality of Life (HRQoL) as appropriate. Patients with identified problems should be referred to appropriate healthcare providers or specialist services for further management.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: This consensus recommendation provides a framework for patient selection, timing and assessment to support a more structured and equitable management of post-intensive care syndrome.

sections.heading: Editorial comment
sections.text: Systematic follow up of ICU survivors after hospital discharge is needed in order to assess long-term patient-centred outcomes. This is a consensus set of recommendations and not a GRADE-based clinical practice guideline for doing this, which can be considered by relevant ICUs.

items.title: Psychosocial Rehabilitation Interventions for Mental Health Disorders: A Systematic Review.
items.authors: Mohanty P, Rahul K, Qureshi M, Sreekanthaswamy S, Sreekanthaswamy N, Chacko S.

sections.text: Mental health disorders (MHD) contribute substantially to long-term disability and social exclusion, requiring interventions that extend beyond symptom reduction to recovery and functional outcomes. This systematic review evaluated psychosocial rehabilitation (PR) interventions for improving functioning, recovery, quality of life (QoL), and service-related outcomes among individuals with MHD. We conducted a structured search of PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, and PsycINFO for studies published between 2015 and 2025 using controlled vocabulary and free-text terms. Eligible studies evaluated PR-focused interventions in clinically diagnosed MHD and reported recovery, functioning, social participation, QoL, service engagement, self-management, or community integration outcomes. We excluded pharmacological-only studies, noninterventional studies, reviews, editorials, conference abstracts, and case reports. Eleven studies were included after screening 252 records. The evidence base comprised randomized and cluster-randomized trials, controlled intervention studies, secondary analyses, feasibility or exploratory studies, long-term follow-up evidence, and one clinical trial protocol, reflecting different levels of evidentiary strength. Although limited to 11 eligible studies, the review captured multiple PR models and outcome domains and was designed as a focused narrative synthesis rather than a definitive pooled comparison. Findings indicated potential benefits of cognitive remediation, CBT-integrated programs, Housing First, peer-led rehabilitation, and digital self-management for negative symptoms, social functioning, housing stability, recovery, and service utilization. Overall, PR appears valuable within recovery-oriented mental health systems, although heterogeneous designs and limited robust comparative evidence warrant cautious interpretation.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: Gaming disorder (GD) is prevalent among adolescents, and those with neurodevelopmental conditions or symptoms of anxiety and depression may be particularly vulnerable to GD. items.title: Psychological impact of body mass index changes in older adults: a 12-year longitudinal study.
items.authors: Chou YC, Cheng FS, Weng SH, Tseng CH, Hu HY, Liu CH.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Significant changes in body mass index (BMI) may be associated with psychological distress, particularly in older adults. However, few longitudinal studies have examined this relationship over time. This study aimed to investigate the association between BMI changes and psychological distress assessed repeatedly among community-dwelling older adults in Taiwan.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: This 12-year prospective cohort study included 70,570 adults aged ≥ 65 years who participated in the Taipei City Government's annual physical examination program between 2005 and 2016. BMI changes were classified relative to baseline (Definition 1) and prior follow-up measurements (Definition 2). Psychological distress was assessed using the Brief Symptom Rating Scale (BSRS-5). Multivariable generalized estimating equation (GEE) models were used to evaluate associations between BMI changes and psychological distress. Sensitivity analyses included a Cox proportional-hazards model treating incident psychological distress (first BSRS-5 ≥ 6) as the outcome, with BMI change as a time-varying covariate, and a lagged model relating BMI change to distress at the subsequent examination.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Under both definitions, participants with major weight loss (> 10%) had the highest risk of psychological distress (Definition 1: adjusted odds ratio [aOR] = 1.90, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.77-2.04; Definition 2: aOR = 1.96, 95% CI: 1.80-2.14). Minor weight loss (5%-10%) also increased the risk (Definition 1: aOR = 1.60, 95% CI: 1.52-1.68; Definition 2: aOR = 1.52, 95% CI: 1.44-1.60). Minor and major weight gains were associated with elevated but comparatively lower risks. In sensitivity analyses, the association between weight loss and psychological distress remained significant and dose-dependent, although attenuated; associations with weight gain were not robust.

sections.text: Weight loss was consistently and dose-dependently associated with psychological distress in older adults and may serve as an early marker of declining health. Regular monitoring of weight change, rather than static weight status, may help prompt timely mental-health screening and nutritional or psychosocial assessment in this population.

items.title: Medication Complexity and Insomnia Severity in Psychiatric Outpatients: A Moderation Analysis Across Mood and Non-Mood Disorders.
items.authors: Martiadis V, Pessina E, Martini A, Marzolla M, Bergesio C, Barbaro F, Cavallo A, Raffone F, Cattaneo CI.

sections.text: Background: Insomnia is common and occurs across psychiatric diagnoses. A prior analysis of this outpatient cohort found that psychotropic medication complexity was associated with insomnia severity, but whether this association is stronger in particular diagnostic groups was not examined. We preregistered a moderation analysis to test whether mood disorder status modifies the association between medication complexity and insomnia, and additionally examined modification by sex and by insomnia domain. Methods: A secondary analysis was performed of cross-sectional, routinely collected data from 502 adult outpatients (from an initial cohort of 506) at an Italian community mental health centre. The primary model regressed the Insomnia Severity Index (ISI) total score on medication complexity × mood disorder status (depressive and bipolar vs. other psychiatric disorders), adjusting for age, sex and education; it was preregistered on the Open Science Framework before any interaction model was estimated. Results: Medication complexity was associated with the ISI total (b = 1.54 per class, 95% CI 0.92 to 2.16; attenuated but retained after benzodiazepine adjustment, b = 1.00, p = 0.009). The prespecified medication complexity × mood interaction was not statistically significant (b = -1.02, 95% CI -2.25 to 0.21, p = 0.103). The medication complexity × sex interaction was also non-significant (b = 0.28, p = 0.64), and the moderation did not differ between ISI domains (three-way interaction p = 0.67). Benzodiazepine prescription was independently associated with the ISI (b = 1.87, p = 0.011). Conclusions: The prespecified hypothesis of a stronger medication complexity-insomnia association in mood disorders was not supported. Because no equivalence margin was prespecified, the analysis cannot establish that the association is equivalent across groups; it indicates only that the hypothesised stronger association was not detected. Findings are exploratory with respect to mechanism and should be read in light of the cross-sectional design and probable confounding by indication.

items.title: National trends and territorial disparities in psychiatry residency fill rates in France: a longitudinal panel study, 2016-2026.
items.authors: Jambas B, Rouxel-Thomat M, Girodeau A, Vadell Martínez J, Endomba FT.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Mental health needs are increasing across Europe, while psychiatric workforce planning in France is challenged by workforce ageing and territorial inequalities.

sections.heading: Objective
sections.text: To assess national trends in psychiatry residency fill rates in France and examine the territorial distribution of unfilled positions from 2016-2017 to 2025-2026.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: We conducted a nationwide retrospective longitudinal panel study including all 28 French residency subdivisions over 10 academic years. Opened and filled positions were extracted from decrees published in the French Official Journal. Fill rates were modelled using a beta-binomial generalised linear mixed model. Heterogeneity was quantified using the median odds ratio, and concentration using the Gini coefficient and top-share estimates.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: The panel included 280 subdivision-year observations, corresponding to 5282 opened, 4719 filled, and 563 unfilled positions. Observed national fill rates declined from near-complete levels before 2019 to 82.49% in 2019-2020 and remained below pre-2019 levels thereafter. The model-based national fill rate decreased from 98.10% in the early period to 82.74% in the late period, an absolute change of -15.4 percentage points. Between-subdivision heterogeneity was substantial. Unfilled positions were territorially concentrated and the top 25% of subdivisions accounted for 61.3% of all unfilled positions.

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: Psychiatry residency underfilling in France has become a sustained, territorially uneven workforce planning issue. In centralised rank-based allocation systems, workforce planning should monitor not only the number of training positions opened, but also their conversion into filled positions and the territorial accumulation of vacancies.

items.title: Psychometric Properties of the Choosing Wisely Questions in a Large Psychiatric Sample.
items.authors: Bengtsson J, Andersson A, Forss Lilja N, Hultgren Farsani I, Lissbrant E, Wettermark B, Blomqvist I.
items.journal: International journal of methods in psychiatric research

sections.heading: Objectives
sections.text: The Choosing Wisely Questions (CWQ) support shared decision-making and aim to reduce low-value care, but their psychometric properties remain unclear. This study evaluated the structural validity, reliability, and item characteristics of the Swedish CWQ in a psychiatric sample.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: In this cross-sectional study, adult patients at a Swedish university psychiatric clinic (early 2025) completed four CWQ items on perceived information about their medication (benefits, risks, alternatives, and no treatment). Structural validity was assessed using exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses. Internal consistency was measured with Cronbach's alpha, and item characteristics were examined using a graded response model.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: A total of 666 patients (57.2% women; median age 35.0 years) were included. The majority had multiple ICD F-diagnoses. EFA supported a one-factor solution explaining 53.8% of the variance. CFA demonstrated excellent model fit (CFI = 0.998, TLI = 0.995, RMSEA = 0.032, SRMR = 0.015). Internal consistency was good (α = 0.81, 95% CI 0.79-0.83). In the item response analysis, all items showed high discrimination (a = 1.94-2.72) and ordered thresholds. Patients reported more information on benefits than on risks, alternatives, or no treatment (p < 0.001).

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: The Swedish CWQ show good validity, reliability, and item performance, supporting their use as a unidimensional measure of perceived information in psychiatric shared decision-making.

items.title: Insights into morbidity and mortality in Gaucher disease: a cohort study.
items.authors: Teixeira LF, Poswar F, Randon DN, Pasqualotto A, Schwartz IVD.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Gaucher disease (GD) is a rare lysosomal disorder classified, on the basis of neurological involvement, into type 1 (GD1, non-neuronopathic) and types 2 (GD2) and 3 (GD3) (neuronopathic). Data on morbidity and mortality in Latin American cohorts remain scarce.

sections.heading: Aims
sections.text: To characterise morbidity and mortality patterns in a Brazilian GD cohort.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: Retrospective cohort study at a single GD referral centre in Porto Alegre, Brazil (2003-2023; n  = 53; GD1 = 45, GD2 = 4, GD3 = 4). Diagnosis was molecularly confirmed by Sanger and massive parallel sequencing of GBA1. Comorbidities and causes of death were retrieved by chart review; survival was estimated by Kaplan-Meier analysis. Results: Median follow-up was 15 years. In GD1, comorbidities were predominantly psychiatric (71%), metabolic/endocrinological (69%) and cardiovascular (60%). Nine patients (17%) died: four GD1 patients (median age 65 years; three from malignancy, one from sepsis), all four GD2 patients (median age 5 months; respiratory or hepatic failure, sepsis) and one GD3 patient (Sudden Unexpected Death in Epilepsy at 27 years).

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: The phenotype-specific mortality pattern - malignancy as the leading cause of death in GD1, uniform early death in GD2 reflecting the disease's neurological trajectory rather than a failure of enzyme replacement therapy, and neurological death in GD3 - underscores the substantial burden of oncological, cardiovascular, metabolic and neurological comorbidities in this population and supports systematic multidisciplinary surveillance as a routine component of GD care in Brazil, even in resource-limited settings.

sections.heading: Take-home message
sections.text: Adult patients with Gaucher disease type 1 require close clinical monitoring for oncological, cardiovascular, metabolic and psychiatric comorbidities. Gaucher disease type 2 remains a devastating disease with a poor prognosis under current therapies.

items.title: Why sleep assessment belongs in the memory clinic.
items.authors: Suraev A, Fernandes M, Lim A, Han F, Naismith SL, Liguori C.
items.journal: Alzheimer's & dementia : the journal of the Alzheimer's Association

sections.text: Sleep disturbances are highly prevalent in older adults and are particularly common among individuals attending memory clinics for assessment of cognitive impairment. Emerging evidence links sleep disorders, including insomnia, obstructive sleep apnea, circadian rhythm disruption, and rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder, to cognitive decline, neurodegenerative pathology, and reduced quality of life for patients and caregivers. Despite their high prevalence and clinical relevance, sleep disturbances are not routinely assessed within many memory clinic and neurologic, psychiatric, and geriatric settings, and approaches to screening, diagnosis, and management vary widely across health-care systems. This Perspective article examines current approaches to sleep assessment and management within memory clinic and specialized settings across four international contexts. We highlight the absence of systematic approaches to identifying and managing sleep disturbances in this population and propose the need for a pragmatic stepped-care framework to improve detection, guide referral pathways, and support more consistent and personalized care in memory clinic settings.

items.title: α-synuclein pathology drives region-specific tau deposition.
items.authors: Hojjati SH, Chiang GC, Wang XH, Khalafi M, Shah S, Zhou L, Keil S, Glodzik L, McIntire LBJ, Tanzi E, Feiz F, Maloney T, Li Y, Butler TA, Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative.
items.journal: Alzheimer's & dementia : the journal of the Alzheimer's Association

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: Dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) is a common but underdiagnosed neurodegenerative disease associated with α-synuclein pathology. Clinically, DLB is characterized by early motor dysfunction and psychiatric symptoms, in contrast to early memory decline typical of Alzheimer's disease (AD). Lewy body and AD pathology commonly co-occur. It remains unclear how α-synuclein pathology, either alone or in combination with AD pathology, produces clinical features considered distinctive of synucleinopathy.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: We analyzed 531 Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative participants using neuroimaging to compare tau deposition patterns between α-synuclein-positive and α-synuclein-negative individuals.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: α-synuclein-positive individuals showed significantly greater tau deposition in basal ganglia (BG), insula, and medial temporal lobe (MTL). Increased tau burden in these regions correlated with more severe psychiatric symptoms and slower reaction times. These associations were present only in the α-synuclein-positive group.

sections.heading: Discussion
sections.text: These results suggest that α-synuclein pathology is associated with region-specific tau positron emission tomography abnormalities that map onto core clinical features of synucleinopathy.

items.title: Parkinson Disease Subtype Stability and Eventual Convergence.
items.authors: Rosok LM, Lessov-Schlaggar CN, Eid AM, Foster ER, Maiti B, Domash H, Hwang H, Perrin RJ, Kotzbauer PT, Perlmutter JS, Campbell MC.
items.journal: Annals of clinical and translational neurology

sections.heading: Objective
sections.text: Previous research identified distinct Parkinson disease (PD) clinical subtypes of "Motor Only," "Psychiatric & Motor," and "Cognitive & Motor" based on comprehensive, multidomain classification. Whether these subtypes reflect distinct trajectories or progressive disease stages remains unknown. This study aimed to determine the longitudinal stability of PD subtype membership.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: This study included 250 PD participants with baseline subtype classifications and behavioral evaluations at two timepoints (average interval = 2.51 years), including motor, cognitive, and psychiatric assessments. Latent transition analyses tested the stability of PD subtype membership over time, and logistic regression models examined baseline factors associated with subtype transitions. Available brain autopsy data from 67 participants strengthened analyses by allowing the exclusion of 9 participants with non-PD neuropathologic diagnoses (e.g., Multiple System Atrophy, Progressive Supranuclear Palsy).

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: The three baseline subtypes ("Motor Only," "Psychiatric & Motor," and "Cognitive & Motor") persisted at the second timepoint. Individuals in the "Motor Only" subtype at baseline had a high probability of remaining in the same subtype at follow-up (0.91), demonstrating longitudinal stability. Participants in the "Psychiatric & Motor" and "Cognitive & Motor" subtypes remained in the same subtype with probabilities of 0.55 and 0.59, respectively. A fourth "Severe Multidomain" subtype emerged at follow-up, characterized by more pronounced motor, cognitive, and psychiatric dysfunction. 64% of the "Severe Multidomain" group had dementia, compared with ≤ 7% in the other three subtypes. Subsequent analyses indicated that higher baseline Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) sum of boxes was strongly associated with transition to a different subtype.

sections.heading: Interpretation
sections.text: These findings suggest that PD subtypes reflect relatively stable subgroups that may eventually converge with development of dementia.

items.title: Study protocol for the Healthier Wealthier Families (HWF) cluster randomised controlled trial: testing the effectiveness and cost-benefits of offering financial counselling to families with young children who report financial hardship at well-child health home visits.

items.title: When You Hear Hoofbeats, It May Still Be the Medication: A Case of Aripiprazole-Induced Hypersexuality Masquerading as Psychiatric Decompensation.
items.authors: Cudjoe N, Jenkins TC, Stallworth B, Mwai CK, Morgan A.

sections.text: Aripiprazole has a known association with impulse-control disorders (ICDs), yet these adverse effects are frequently underrecognized and misattributed to psychiatric decompensation, particularly in women. We report a case of a 27-year-old African American woman with schizoaffective disorder who developed marked, new-onset hypersexual behavior temporally associated with aripiprazole. Aripiprazole accounts for a majority of ICDs reported among this class of antipsychotics, likely due to its D2/D3 partial agonism. This case highlights the critical need for clinicians to maintain a high index of suspicion for medication-induced ICDs when patients develop new impulsive or compulsive behaviors.

items.title: Network Neuroanatomy of Self-Awareness: A Narrative Review of Self-Referential Processing, Metacognition, and Embodiment.
items.authors: Kandilas A, Samolis A, Kalamatianos T, Margaritis I, Tsakotos G, Triantafyllou G, Piagkou M.

sections.text: Self-awareness encompasses the capacity to recognize and evaluate information about oneself, including mental states, actions, autobiographical history, and bodily experience. Although closely related to consciousness, autobiographical memory, metacognition, clinical insight, anosognosia, and bodily self-consciousness, these constructs are not interchangeable. This focused narrative review synthesizes human neuroanatomical and neuroimaging evidence identified through a targeted PubMed/MEDLINE search covering January 1997 to August 15, 2026, supplemented by reference-chain searching. To improve methodological transparency, the revised review specifies eligibility principles, the narrative synthesis strategy, and reproducible domain-specific Boolean search strings; because the article is a narrative rather than a systematic review, no protocol registration, PRISMA screening flow, formal study-level risk-of-bias assessment, or quantitative pooling was undertaken. The evidence is organized into four interacting domains: self-referential representation, autobiographical continuity, metacognitive monitoring, and embodied self-processing. Cortical midline and default mode regions are prominent in self-referential evaluation; medial temporal systems support autobiographical information; anterior and lateral prefrontal and frontoparietal regions contribute to monitoring and updating; and temporoparietal, precuneal, insular, and sensorimotor regions contribute to bodily self-processing. Importantly, these macroscopic territories overlap and contain functionally heterogeneous subregions, so the proposed mappings represent network-weighted tendencies rather than one-to-one anatomical assignments. Clinical findings further show that anosognosia in Alzheimer's disease, impaired insight in schizophrenia, altered self-experience in depersonalization-derealization disorder, and awareness deficits after acquired brain injury (ABI) involve different combinations of these processes. We therefore propose a representation-memory-monitoring-embodiment framework as a heuristic neuroanatomical synthesis, not a diagnostic or treatment model. Its value lies in separating constructs often grouped under the term self-awareness and in generating testable hypotheses for longitudinal multimodal imaging, lesion mapping, causal studies, and construct-matched interventions.

items.title: Testing Continuous Age as an Effect Modifier of the Association Between Diminished Ikigai and Psychological Distress in Two Long-Term Disaster Contexts in Japan.
items.authors: Omori T, Iwai M.

sections.heading: Background/objectives
sections.text: Mental-health research often represents chronological age as a threshold or adjustment variable, although psychosocial associations may vary across adulthood. We tested whether continuous age modified the association between a context-specific single-item indicator of diminished ikigai and psychological distress in two Japanese communities with long-term disaster consequences. The ikigai indicators differed by context and were not treated as equivalent multidimensional measures.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: Secondary cross-sectional analyses used Miyakejima 2020/21 ( N = 158; complete-case n = 147) and Okuma 2024 ( N = 134; 111 valid 28-item General Health Questionnaire (GHQ-28) classifications; complete-case n = 110). Age-by-ikigai interactions were primary; fixed <65/≥65 analyses and robustness checks were secondary or exploratory.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: In Miyakejima, the estimated interaction odds ratio (OR) was 2.00 per 10 years (95% confidence interval [CI] [1.03, 3.91], p = 0.042; likelihood-ratio p = 0.029), with substantial uncertainty at age extremes; the threshold interaction was unsupported. In Okuma, low/absent ikigai was associated with GHQ-28 high-risk status (OR = 12.94, 95% CI [4.96, 33.8], p < 0.001), while age modification was not detected (interaction OR = 0.88, 95% CI [0.44, 1.76], p = 0.711). The historical Miyakejima reanalysis also did not provide detectable evidence of corresponding modification.

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: Within these context-specific samples, continuous-age modelling yielded preliminary evidence of heterogeneity in Miyakejima not captured by a 65-year threshold. Larger longitudinal studies should evaluate this signal's precision and transferability.

items.title: 'I Am a Person Before My Label': Exploring People's Perceptions of Different Discourses Associated With Dyslexia.
items.authors: Macdonald SJ, Pearson A, Botha M, Leigh J, Williams K, Williams G, Spaeth E, Rose K, Memmott A, Grant A.

sections.text: Language plays a central role in shaping how dyslexia is understood and negotiated across education, employment and everyday life. While debates have historically focused on diagnosis, less attention has been given to how adults who identify as dyslexic interpret and evaluate the labels applied to them. This article examines dyslexic adults' perceptions of dyslexia-related and neurodiversity movement terminology, drawing on a UK mixed-methods survey of 166 participants who identified as dyslexic, with or without co-occurring neurodivergences. Quantitative findings reveal a clear hierarchy of label preference. Participants strongly favoured dyslexia-specific, identity-based terms such as 'dyslexic', while rejecting broader, deficit-centred labels including 'learning difficulty', 'specific learning disability' and 'specific learning disorder'. Qualitative analysis shows these preferences are shaped by experiences of stigma and misrecognition. The findings show that adoption of a neurodivergent label varies depending on whether participants have single or multiple neurodivergent identities. Those with dyslexia alone expressed greater ambivalence towards the label of neurodiversity. In contrast, dyslexic participants alongside autism or ADHD were more likely to adopt the label. The study highlights the importance of listening to dyslexic voices in debates about terminology. It cautions against deficit-based and overly generalised language which risks reproducing stigma rather than challenging oppression.

items.title: Measurement Heterogeneity and Pooled Prevalence of Academic Procrastination Among Health Sciences Students: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
items.authors: Vera-Ponce VJ, Zuzunaga-Montoya FE, Cómina-Tamayo MJ, León-Figueroa DA, Uceda CIG, Rivera-Lozada O, Ballena-Caicedo J, Delgado-Toro HE, Valladares-Garrido MJ.
items.journal: European journal of investigation in health, psychology and education
items.journal_abbrev: Eur J Investig Health Psychol Educ

sections.heading: Background/objectives
sections.text: In health sciences students, academic procrastination can affect performance, mental health, and professional development. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to estimate the pooled prevalence of study-defined elevated academic procrastination among health sciences students and to describe the methodological and measurement characteristics of the instruments used to assess it.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: A systematic review with meta-analysis was conducted. We included observational studies reporting the prevalence of academic procrastination among undergraduate students enrolled in health sciences programs, including medicine, nursing, dentistry, psychology, and related health professions. The reported measurement characteristics of the instruments used to assess academic procrastination, including validity, reliability, and cut-off criteria, were reviewed and systematized. The meta-analysis was performed employing a random-effects model and the double arcsine transformation (Freeman-Tukey) to stabilize variance. Subgroup analyses and meta-regressions were calculated to explore possible sources of variation.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Twenty-six studies were included with a total of 8211 students. The pooled prevalence of study-defined elevated academic procrastination was 55.35% (95% CI: 46.55-63.98%, I^2 = 98%). The prevalence was higher in nursing students (62.60%), followed by psychology (61.67%), medicine (52.62%), and dentistry (45.76%). The most commonly used instruments were the Procrastination Assessment Scale for Students (38.5%), Academic Procrastination Scale (23.1%), Tuckman's Procrastination Scale or its adaptations (15.4%), Academic Procrastination Scale by McCloskey and Scielzo or related APS versions (11.5%), Lay's Procrastination Scale (7.7%), and MHCA (3.8%). Most studies used non-probabilistic sampling, and only 8% validated instruments specifically for their target populations. Reliability coefficients were generally adequate (α = 0.75-0.95). The meta-regression revealed a slight upward trend in prevalence as a function of publication year, although this was not statistically significant.

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: Academic procrastination appears to be frequent among health sciences students; however, the pooled estimate should be interpreted as a descriptive summary of study-defined prevalence rather than as a universal prevalence estimate, given the very high between-study heterogeneity and the variability in instruments, cut-off criteria, and population-specific validation. Educational institutions should implement prevention and support strategies, while research should prioritize instrument validation, measurement standardization, and transparent case definition criteria.

items.title: Risk and Protective Factors of Food Insecurity Among Children in Low-Income Families in the United States: Application of the Multiple Disadvantage Model.
items.authors: Cheng TC, Lo CC.
items.journal: European journal of investigation in health, psychology and education
items.journal_abbrev: Eur J Investig Health Psychol Educ

sections.text: This study investigated relationships between low-income children's food insecurity and five factors: social disorganization, social structural factors, social relationships, health/mental health, and access to services. A sample of 12,215 low-income children and parents was extracted from the 2021 National Survey of Children's Health. Logistic regression results showed the likelihood of such children's food insecurity to be associated positively with several factors: racial discrimination, child aged 6-10 years, child aged 11-13 years, child aged 14-17 years, Black child, child's chronic health condition, family member mental health problem, Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program participation, receipt of Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children, and lunch program participation. As well, children's food insecurity likelihood was associated negatively with parents' age and education, neighbor support, parents' general health and mental health, and receipt of Temporary Assistance for Needy Families. Research implications include interventions at the individual level (e.g., screening for food insecurity, treatment of sick or mentally ill family members), community level (e.g., food pantries, neighbor support network), and macro level (e.g., advocating for racial/ethnic minorities, expanding cash and food benefits).

items.title: Climate Change and Pediatric Gastrointestinal Health: A Narrative Review.
items.authors: Kuhn A, Dugar S, Shah M, Philipsborn R.

sections.text: In 2025, the United Nations acknowledged that the world has failed to reduce carbon emissions sufficiently to avoid 1.5C warming-the level set by the Paris Accords to avoid devastating consequences. Communities already feel the implications of climate change, and it is creating new challenges for patients and health-care teams. While global efforts to reduce emissions and prevent the worst consequences of climate change persist, efforts to understand and adapt to the current and near-term consequences of climate change are also vital. Climate change is contributing to more frequent and severe weather events and compounding other ecological changes, with immediate and downstream implications for health. Pediatric patients are particularly vulnerable to the impacts of climate change, given their physiology, behaviors, ongoing development, and dependence on caregivers. This narrative review focuses on the implications of climate change for pediatric gastrointestinal (GI) health, elucidating key pathways by which climate change intersects with GI health that emerge from the literature. These pathways include heat-related illness and prenatal exposure to extreme heat, health implications of climate-driven migration and displacement, changing patterns of infectious GI diseases, the effects of pollution on noncommunicable GI diseases, the impacts of climate change on mental health and the gut-brain axis, and exacerbation of food insecurity and malnutrition. By understanding risks to their patients from these pathways, pediatric GI professionals may be better poised to assess for climate-driven exposures and to address patient care needs related to climate change. Pediatric GI professionals also have an opportunity as a community to engage in the needed health-care sector transformation to sustainable care delivery, bolster the resilience of health-care infrastructure, and advocate for policies to protect pediatric patients.

items.title: Subjective cognitive decline and cognitive leisure activity engagement in older adults: a mixed-methods study.
items.authors: Akbayrak E, Powell PA, Barnes S.

sections.heading: Background and objectives
sections.text: Subjective cognitive decline (SCD), self-perceived worsening in cognitive abilities without objective impairment, is an early marker of dementia linked to poorer mental health and reduced quality of life. Cognitive leisure activities (CLA) are low-cost, accessible behaviors that support cognitive functioning and well-being. However, evidence remains limited regarding the directionality, mechanisms, and domain-specific nature of the SCD-CLA relationship. This study provides novel mixed-methods evidence to inform early, person-centered intervention strategies.

sections.heading: Research design and methods
sections.text: A sequential explanatory mixed-methods design combined a cross-sectional survey of 255 older adults and semi-structured interviews with 20 individuals living with SCD in the United Kingdom. Quantitative data were analyzed using regression analyses, and qualitative data through thematic analysis. Results were integrated via a joint display.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Quantitative analyses showed higher SCD concerns were associated with lower CLA engagement, with specific activity types linked to distinct cognitive domains. Qualitative findings highlighted motivations, barriers, and strategies shaping engagement, including enjoyment, social connection, and emotional or health-related challenges. Integrated findings indicated potential reciprocal influences: cognitive concerns could motivate CLA engagement to maintain cognitive health, but SCD-related emotional distress and reduced confidence constrained participation. CLA did not statistically moderate the age-SCD association, yet participants reported perceived cognitive and emotional benefits.

sections.heading: Discussion and implications
sections.text: These findings highlight the need for interventions that move beyond simple activity promotion to address emotional ambivalence, stigma, and contextual barriers to participation. Tailoring CLA opportunities to individual preferences and capacities may enhance engagement, cognitive wellbeing, and emotional resilience in later life.

items.title: Prenatal maternal inflammation and cognitive performance in offspring during late midlife.
items.authors: Hoffman LJ, Smith EC, Pike MR, Kring AM, Breen EC, Cohn BA, Cirillo PM, Krigbaum NY, Cogan AB, Patwardhan BP, Olino TM, Olson IR, Ellman LM.

sections.text: Higher levels of prenatal maternal inflammation (PNMI) have been associated with offspring psychiatric disorders characterized by cognitive changes, and alterations in cognitive ability during early stages of development. Investigations into the effects of PNMI exposure and timing on cognitive outcomes in offspring later in life are lacking. Thus, the current study aimed to assess whether PNMI exposure in the first two trimesters was associated with offspring cognitive performance in late midlife. Participants were 137 mother-offspring dyads from the Child Health and Developmental Studies (CHDS) cohort that had maternal first and second trimester (T1, T2) sera data for interleukin- (IL-) 6, IL-8, IL-1 receptor antagonist (RA), and soluble tumor necrosis factor receptor-II (sTNF-RII), and an offspring follow-up assessment during late midlife (ages 57-62). Offspring underwent a battery of cognitive tests assessing verbal memory, general cognitive ability, verbal IQ, executive control, attention, working memory, and fine motor functioning. After controlling for maternal education to account for postnatal cognitive advantage, we identified a significant association between higher T1 PNMI and better performance on tasks of executive control (IL-8, Trails B-A, p = .003) and working memory (sTNF-RII, Digit-Span [DS] Backwards, p = .014). We also found significant associations between higher T2 PNMI and poorer performance on executive control (IL-6, Trails B-A, p = .002), working memory (IL-6, DS Backwards, p = .018), verbal IQ (IL-6, Wechsler Test of Adult Reading [WTAR], p = .039), and verbal memory (IL-8, Long Delay-Free Recall [LD-FR], p = .001). Such timing-specific associations of PNMI suggest that early gestational inflammatory exposure may be protective for some cognitive capacities, whereas mid-gestational exposure, especially to IL-6, suggests risk for decreases in memory and several other cognitive domains measurable in offspring approximately six decades later.

items.title: Biological Mechanisms Underlying the Adverse Health Consequences of Human Circadian Misalignment from Night Shift Work.
items.authors: Lundholm KR, Satterfield BC, Banks S, Liu PY, Kombala CJ, Hurtado-Alvarado G, Greer AJ, Muck RA, Layton MA, Du D, Gaddameedhi S, Van Dongen HPA.

sections.heading: Purpose of review
sections.text: The waking and working times of night shift workers are displaced relative to the natural light/dark cycle, putting behavioral patterns in misalignment with the circadian regulation of biological processes. This state of circadian misalignment constitutes a circadian health problem, with widespread negative consequences for metabolic, cardiovascular, and mental health, as well as elevated risk of cancer. Scientific advances over the past decade have shed light on key aspects of the underlying biological mechanisms. With a focus on recent human studies, this paper reviews novel insights into what drives the adverse health consequences of circadian misalignment due to night shift work.

sections.heading: Recent findings
sections.text: Misalignment between the central circadian pacemaker and externally driven behavioral patterns during night shift work produces a rapid uncoupling of peripheral rhythms, reflected in the cargo of exosomes and other signaling mechanisms, and causes conflict between central and peripheral regulatory mechanisms. This endogenous internal desynchrony has been shown to be linked to shifted meal timing and, in part, may be mediated by the gut microbiome. Endogenous internal desynchrony leads to insulin resistance - a manifestation of metabolic dysfunction. It perturbs the cardiometabolic and immune systems, and also erodes mental health. At the cellular level, mistimed DNA repair mechanisms leave residual DNA damage after exposure to a night shift schedule - which, over time, may result in genomic instability and ultimately carcinogenesis.

sections.heading: Summary
sections.text: A systems biology perspective serves to elucidate how the effects of endogenous circadian disruption from night shift work increase the risk of acute and chronic illnesses. Internal desynchrony, endogenous in nature, is a common underlying cause. Time-restricted eating may help to address metabolic dysfunction due to night shift work; countermeasures for other negative health outcomes, including cancer and mental health disorders, remain to be developed.

items.title: Stroke Mimics in a Tertiary Comprehensive Stroke Center: Implications for Healthcare Provider Education.
items.authors: Abbasi MH, Helson A, Penafiel A, Wang AS, Miulli DE, Khan FS.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: The proportion of stroke mimics in code stroke activation varies. Decreasing the number of stroke mimics requires clinicians to master the skills needed to distinguish strokes from stroke mimics. There is a lack of quality initiatives to produce such astute clinicians, who, once trained, should improve the accuracy of stroke alerts, reduce patient risk from unnecessary radiation, optimize resource utilization, and correctly diagnose patients to provide the best treatment course.

sections.heading: Methodology
sections.text: As a comprehensive stroke program, stroke data were collected as part of the continuous quality control and improvement procedures. A retrospective study from January 2026 to June 2026 was conducted using the original stroke database to select patients with code stroke activation who were treated with the code stroke protocol and their final diagnoses at discharge. No individual patient data were reviewed. No inferential statistical analyses were performed.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: From January 2026 to June 2026, there were a total of 630 code stroke activations (mean = 105 patients/month; range = 86-120 patients). True strokes accounted for 35.1% (221/630, 35.1%) of the code stroke activations, yielding 64.9% (409/630, 64.9%) stroke mimics. Among stroke patients, 110/630 (17.5%) were ischemic strokes, 96/630 (15.2%) were transient ischemic attacks, 14/630 (2.2%) were intracerebral hemorrhages, and 1/630 (0.2%) was a subarachnoid hemorrhage. The stroke mimics were sepsis (36/630, 5.7%), migraine (29/630, 4.6%), seizure (21/630, 3.3%), subdural hematoma (21/630, 3.3%), hypertensive emergency/crisis (21/630, 3.3%), residual deficits from prior stroke (18/630, 2.9%), unruptured aneurysm (13/630, 2.1%), alcohol abuse/other drug use/mental illness (12/630, 1.9%), Bell's palsy (9/630, 1.4%), and all other diagnoses (229/630, 36.3%).

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: In this study, stroke mimics accounted for 409/630 (64.9%) of code stroke activations, which is higher than documented in the literature and in past performance at this institution. The most likely stroke mimics are sepsis, migraine, seizure, subdural hematoma, and hypertensive emergency/crisis. Parallel increases in public awareness and education on stroke and lifelong education on acute stroke recognition must continue for all clinicians to accurately identify patients with acute strokes, for which a large amount of hospital resources is used for code stroke activation. Future studies should investigate methods to efficiently diagnose patients and optimize healthcare resources.

items.title: Circadian-Based Optimization of Pharmacotherapy in Chronic Diseases: Integrating Pharmacokinetics, Pharmacodynamics, and Disease Rhythm.
items.authors: C M, Mehrotra S, Srivastava N, Jain A, Dixit R.

sections.text: Circadian rhythms are endogenous, approximately 24-hour biological cycles that regulate physiological processes, including cardiovascular function, metabolism, immune activity, endocrine signaling, and sleep-wake patterns. These rhythms significantly influence disease pathophysiology and therapeutic responses, making biological time an important determinant of treatment outcomes. Several chronic diseases, including cardiovascular disorders, asthma, rheumatoid arthritis, metabolic syndrome, and psychiatric conditions, exhibit predictable circadian variations in symptom severity and disease activity. Simultaneously, circadian oscillations affect pharmacokinetic processes such as drug absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion, as well as pharmacodynamic mechanisms involving receptor sensitivity and cellular responsiveness. As a result, identical drug doses administered at different times may produce considerable differences in efficacy and toxicity. This review analyzes the role of circadian biology in optimizing pharmacotherapy through the integration of chronopharmacology and chronotherapy. It discusses the molecular basis of circadian regulation and its influence on physiological systems, pharmacokinetics, and pharmacodynamics. Disease-specific chronotherapeutic applications in cardiovascular, metabolic, endocrine, respiratory, rheumatologic, psychiatric, and oncologic disorders are highlighted. Clinical examples, including evening statin administration, timed bronchodilator use, and modified-release glucocorticoid therapy, highlight the practical benefits of circadian-based therapies. However, evidence remains variable across therapeutic areas, with some chronotherapeutic strategies, such as bedtime antihypertensive dosing, showing conflicting results in recent clinical trials. Further research is needed to define optimal timing recommendations and facilitate wider clinical adoption. Throughout, the strength of evidence is appraised to distinguish chronotherapeutic strategies with sufficient support for routine clinical use from those that remain experimental. The review also discusses emerging developments in chronopharmacokinetic modeling, advanced drug delivery systems, wearable monitoring devices, and precision chronomedicine. Despite promising evidence, broader implementation remains limited by variability in circadian patterns, lack of awareness, and insufficient standardized guidelines. Integrating circadian principles into pharmacotherapy and, ultimately, combining precision chronotherapy with lifestyle-based strategies may offer a promising direction for improving therapeutic precision, disease prevention, and patient outcomes.

items.title: Mental Health Literacy Among Future Health and Education Professionals: Validity Evidence of the Spanish Version of the Mental Health Literacy Questionnaire for Young Adults.
items.authors: Rodríguez-Medina J, Alcover Van de Walle C, San Martín González P, González-Sanguino C.
items.journal: European journal of investigation in health, psychology and education
items.journal_abbrev: Eur J Investig Health Psychol Educ

sections.text: Mental health literacy (MHL) plays a crucial role in the early identification, management, and prevention of mental health problems, especially among young adults. For future health and education professionals, robust MHL is a foundational component of clinical readiness, ensuring they are adequately prepared to recognize early signs of psychological distress, mitigate stigma, and facilitate timely referrals in healthcare and community settings. This study aimed to examine the internal structure and psychometric properties of the Mental Health Literacy Questionnaire for Young Adults (MHLq-YA) within a Spanish university population. An initial sample of 425 university students enrolled in Nursing and Education programs was recruited. Following data screening for invariant and aberrant responding, the final analytical sample comprised 416 participants. Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA) supported a four-factor structure (Knowledge, Stereotypes, Help-Seeking, and Self-Help) with an adequate and structural fit to the data, supporting its multidimensionality with an adequate model fit (CFI = 0.949, TLI = 0.944, RMSEA = 0.068). Evidence of convergent and discriminant validity was observed in three of the four dimensions, while the relationship between Knowledge and Self-Help warranted theoretical interpretation. Convergent validity was supported for three dimensions (Stereotypes, Help-Seeking, and Self-Help), whereas the Knowledge dimension showed comparatively weaker convergent validity (AVE = 0.436). Discriminant validity was supported for all factor pairs under the HTMT criterion, although the stricter Fornell-Larcker criterion was not met for the Knowledge-Self-Help pair, reflecting a conceptual and empirical overlap between these two dimensions that is discussed as a structural limitation of the model. Item Response Theory (IRT) analyses revealed high measurement precision in the lower and moderate ranges of the latent traits, particularly for the Help-Seeking and Self-Help subscales. Ceiling effects and cross-loadings in specific items were resolved through a stepwise model re-specification. The final 26-item version demonstrated robust psychometric performance. These findings support the MHLq-YA as a valid and reliable tool for assessing mental health literacy in academic settings. Crucially, it allows educators to identify gaps in clinical preparedness before students interact with actual patients or vulnerable populations. Ultimately, these results inform targeted interventions to improve mental health awareness, help-seeking behavior, and the overall quality of future clinical care provided by university students.
